pool.name: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)
pool.origin: Alistair Cockburn (2005; originally on the Portland Pattern Repository wiki)
pool.whatItIs: The original article defining ports and adapters: the application talks to the outside world only through ports (purposeful conversations owned by the app), and each port has N interchangeable adapters (HTTP, CLI, test double, real DB, in-memory DB). Cockburn's stated goal is that the application can be driven equally by users, programs, automated tests, or batch scripts, and developed and tested in isolation from runtime devices and databases.
pool.concreteDirective: Declare every external interaction as a port interface owned by the application layer, and put the technology in an adapter under `adapters/` that implements it. Files under `domain/` or `application/` MUST NOT import anything from `adapters/`, `infrastructure/`, or `infra/`. Every driven port must ship with at least two adapters: the real one and an in-memory/fake one used by tests — if a port has only one adapter, the abstraction is unearned; inline it.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: inner layers must not import outer layers
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '(^|/)(domain|application)/' || true)
[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0
fail=0
for f in $files; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  if grep -nE "(from|import|require|use )[^\"']*[\"'][^\"']*(adapters?|infrastructure|infra)/" "$f"; then
    echo "hexagonal: $f (inner layer) imports an outer adapter/infrastructure module" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
exit $fail

pool.name: The Clean Architecture (The Dependency Rule)
pool.origin: Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob), Clean Coder Blog, 13 Aug 2012; expanded in the 2017 book Clean Architecture
pool.whatItIs: The post that unified Hexagonal, Onion, DCI and BCE into concentric circles (Entities / Use Cases / Interface Adapters / Frameworks & Drivers) governed by one overriding constraint: "source code dependencies can only point inwards" and "the name of something declared in an outer circle must not be mentioned by the code in an inner circle."
pool.concreteDirective: Enforce the Dependency Rule literally at the identifier level: no framework, ORM, HTTP, or driver type name (Express/Fastify/NestJS, Prisma/TypeORM/Sequelize/Mongoose, Django/Flask/SQLAlchemy, `net/http`, `database/sql`, GORM, boto3, `pg`, `redis`) may appear in any file under `domain/` or `application/` — not in an import, a type annotation, a field, or a function signature. Cross every boundary with a plain data structure defined by the inner circle; never pass a Request, Row, Model, or Entity object outward or inward unchanged.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: no framework/ORM/transport names inside the core
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
DENY='express|fastify|@nestjs|axios|prisma|typeorm|sequelize|mongoose|knex|django|flask|sqlalchemy|boto3|net/http|database/sql|gorm|redis|\bpg\b'
files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '(^|/)(domain|entities|usecases|application)/' || true)
[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0
fail=0
for f in $files; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  if grep -nEi "^[[:space:]]*(import|from|require|use)[^;]*($DENY)" "$f"; then
    echo "dependency-rule: $f names an outer-circle technology" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
exit $fail

pool.name: The Onion Architecture (Part 1)
pool.whatItIs: Palermo's layering model whose premise is that it controls coupling: "all code can depend on layers more central, but code cannot depend on layers further out from the core." Its distinctive contribution over classic n-tier is that the interfaces (repositories, gateways) are declared in the domain core and the database is an outer, swappable ring rather than the foundation.
pool.concreteDirective: Declare every repository/gateway interface in the innermost domain package alongside the type it returns, and place the implementation in the outermost infrastructure package. Wire all implementations to interfaces in exactly ONE composition root (`main`, `bootstrap`, `container`) — no service locator lookups, no `new SqlOrderRepository()` anywhere but that file. The database schema is not the source of truth for the model; if a domain type changes only because a column changed, the layering is inverted.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: concrete infrastructure classes may only be constructed in the composition root
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
ROOT='(main|bootstrap|container|composition[-_]root|wire)\.'
files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -vE "$ROOT" | grep -E '\.(ts|js|py|go|java|rb|cs)$' || true)
fail=0
for f in $files; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  if grep -nE 'new [A-Za-z]*(Sql|Postgres|Mysql|Mongo|Redis|Http)[A-Za-z]*(Repository|Gateway|Client)\(' "$f"; then
    echo "onion: $f constructs a concrete adapter outside the composition root" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
exit $fail

pool.name: Domain-Driven Design Reference (Definitions and Pattern Summaries)
pool.origin: Eric Evans / Domain Language, Inc. — free CC BY 4.0 companion to the 2004 "blue book" (Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software); index at https://www.domainlanguage.com/ddd/
pool.whatItIs: Evans' own one-page-per-pattern summary of every DDD pattern, including Ubiquitous Language, Bounded Context, Context Map, Anti-Corruption Layer, Aggregate, Entity, Value Object, Domain Event and Repository — the canonical, citable wording for each definition, plus three patterns added after the blue book.
pool.concreteDirective: Name types, methods and events with the exact words domain experts use — if the business says "policy lapses", the method is `lapse()`, never `setStatus(3)`; a term that appears in code but not in conversation with the expert is a modelling bug. Give every top-level deliverable (service, app, top-level package) one explicit Bounded Context with its own model and its own Ubiquitous Language, and do not import a type across a context boundary unless the two contexts have an agreed Shared Kernel or Published Language. At every integration with a legacy system or third-party API where you are the downstream client, put an Anticorruption Layer — an isolating translation layer owned by the consuming context that exposes the upstream system's functionality in terms of your own model — so their vocabulary never leaks past the adapter.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: no cross-context type imports (each top-level dir under contexts/ is a bounded context)
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '^(src/)?contexts/[^/]+/' || true)
[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0
fail=0
for f in $files; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  own=$(printf '%s' "$f" | sed -E 's#^(src/)?contexts/([^/]+)/.*#\2#')
  if grep -nE "[\"'][^\"']*contexts/" "$f" | grep -v "contexts/$own/"; then
    echo "ddd: $f reaches into another bounded context; translate via an anti-corruption layer" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
exit $fail

pool.name: Effective Aggregate Design (Parts I–III)
pool.origin: Vaughn Vernon, 2011 essays for dddcommunity.org; precursor to Implementing Domain-Driven Design (the "red book", 2013). Part I PDF: https://www.dddcommunity.org/wp-content/uploads/files/pdf_articles/Vernon_2011_1.pdf
pool.whatItIs: The three-part essay that turned aggregates from vague advice into four rules of thumb: (1) model true invariants inside consistency boundaries, (2) design small aggregates, (3) reference other aggregates by identity only, (4) update other aggregates using eventual consistency. Part II is where "reference by identity" and the one-transaction-per-aggregate constraint are argued in detail.
pool.concreteDirective: Hold other aggregate roots by ID, never by object reference: a field is `customerId: CustomerId`, never `customer: Customer`. Modify exactly ONE aggregate instance per transaction — if a use case must change two, commit the first and drive the second from a domain event with eventual consistency, and say so in the handler's name. An aggregate that needs a collection sized by user-generated data (orders, comments, line items unbounded) is too big: split it and reference by ID.

pool.name: The C4 model for visualising software architecture
pool.origin: Simon Brown (created 2006–2011); companion book "The C4 Model for Visualising Software Architecture"
pool.whatItIs: A four-level hierarchy of architecture diagrams — System Context, Container, Component, Code — designed as a lightweight alternative to UML, with an explicit notation checklist: every element carries a name, a type, and a technology, every relationship is labelled with intent and protocol, and every diagram carries a title and a key so it stands alone.
pool.concreteDirective: When asked to explain or document a system, produce diagrams at a declared C4 level and never mix abstraction levels in one picture. Every element must state its type explicitly (Person, Software System, Container, Component) plus a short description of its responsibilities, and every container and component must also state its technology — e.g. `Order API [Container: Go] — accepts and prices customer orders`. Every line is a unidirectional relationship labelled with intent, specific rather than a bare "Uses" (e.g. `Reads pricing from`), and any inter-container line must also name the technology/protocol (e.g. `[JSON/HTTPS]`). Every diagram needs a title naming its type and scope ("System Context diagram for My Software System") and a key/legend explaining the notation. Start at System Context and only descend to Container/Component when the reader has asked a question the higher level cannot answer.

pool.name: Documenting Architecture Decisions
pool.whatItIs: The post that invented the ADR: "a short text file in a format similar to an Alexandrian pattern", one file per decision, with the sections Title, Status (proposed / accepted / deprecated / superseded), Context (the forces in play), Decision (in active voice: "We will…"), and Consequences (both good and bad). Its key rule is immutability: an accepted ADR is never rewritten, only superseded by a new one.
pool.concreteDirective: Write an ADR before implementing any decision that is costly to reverse — persistence engine, transport/protocol, auth model, framework, service boundary, consistency model. One decision per file; Nygard's own post prescribes `doc/arch/adr-NNN.md`, but use the adr-tools convention `doc/adr/NNNN-kebab-title.md` for tooling compatibility, with `## Status`, `## Context`, `## Decision`, `## Consequences`. Phrase the decision in active voice ("We will …") and list negative and neutral consequences too, not only positive ones. Number ADRs sequentially and monotonically and never reuse a number. Never rewrite an accepted ADR: add a new one and mark the old one superseded with a reference to its replacement.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: staged ADRs must follow the Nygard filename and section template
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
adrs=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '^doc(s)?/(adr|architecture/decisions)/.*\.md$' || true)
[ -z "$adrs" ] && exit 0
fail=0
for f in $adrs; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  case "${f##*/}" in
    [0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-*.md) ;;
    *) echo "adr: $f must be named NNNN-kebab-title.md" >&2; fail=1 ;;
  esac
  for h in Status Context Decision Consequences; do
    grep -qE "^#{1,3}[[:space:]]*$h" "$f" || { echo "adr: $f is missing a '$h' section" >&2; fail=1; }
  done
done
exit $fail

pool.name: adr-tools (npryce) and the ADR template catalog (joelparkerhenderson)
pool.origin: Nat Pryce (adr-tools, shell CLI) and Joel Parker Henderson (template + example catalog at https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/architecture-decision-record)
pool.whatItIs: adr-tools is a dependency-free shell CLI that creates `doc/adr/`, seeds `0001-record-architecture-decisions.md` linking Nygard's article, numbers records sequentially, and wires up `adr new -s N` to write the reciprocal "Superseded by" link in both files. Henderson's repo is the widely-forked catalog of ADR templates (Nygard, MADR, Tyree & Akerman, Y-statements, business-case) and worked examples.
pool.concreteDirective: Bootstrap ADRs with `adr init doc/adr` when the directory does not exist (`doc/adr` is also the default when no argument is given), and always create records via `adr new "Title"` / `adr new -s <n> "Title"` (or `adr new -l "5:Amends:Amended by"` for non-supersession links) so numbering stays monotonic and links are written on BOTH records. Note that adr-tools writes the MISSPELLED strings "Superceded by" and "Supercedes" (c, not s) — match both spellings in any hook or grep. Pick exactly one template for the repo — record that choice in ADR-0001 — and never mix Nygard and MADR formats in the same directory. If adr-tools is not installed, fall back to writing the file by hand in the same format (`NNNN-kebab-slug.md`, `# NUMBER. TITLE`, `Date: YYYY-MM-DD`, `## Status/Context/Decision/Consequences`) rather than inventing a new one.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: reject duplicate or gapped ADR numbers, and dangling supersession links
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
dir=doc/adr
[ -d "$dir" ] || dir=doc/architecture/decisions
[ -d "$dir" ] || exit 0
dups=$(ls "$dir" 2>/dev/null | sed -nE 's/^([0-9]{4})-.*\.md$/\1/p' | sort | uniq -d)
if [ -n "$dups" ]; then
  echo "adr: duplicate ADR numbers: $dups (use 'adr new' to allocate)" >&2
  exit 1
fi
fail=0
for f in "$dir"/[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-*.md; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  for n in $(sed -nE 's/.*[Ss]uperseded by \[?[Aa][Dd][Rr][ -]?0*([0-9]+).*/\1/p' "$f"); do
    ls "$dir"/$(printf '%04d' "$n")-*.md >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "adr: $f supersedes ADR-$n which does not exist" >&2; fail=1; }
  done
done
exit $fail

pool.name: The Twelve-Factor App
pool.origin: Adam Wiggins / Heroku (2011); source at https://github.com/heroku/12factor. Successor: the community-governed rewrite open-sourced Nov 2024 at https://github.com/twelve-factor/twelve-factor, which will replace the text at 12factor.net
pool.whatItIs: The twelve-point methodology for services deployed to the cloud: one codebase tracked in revision control with many deploys; explicit isolated dependency declaration; strict separation of config from code ("store config in the environment"); backing services as attached resources addressed by URL; strict separate build/release/run stages; stateless processes; port binding; concurrency via the process model; disposability with fast startup and graceful shutdown; dev/prod parity; logs as an event stream written to stdout; admin processes as one-off runs of the same release.
pool.concreteDirective: Read every deploy-varying value (credentials, hostnames, feature flags, ports) from environment variables at process start and fail loudly at boot if one is missing — never from a committed config file, never from a `if env == 'prod'` branch. Write logs unbuffered to stdout as an event stream: no log files, no rotation, no log-path config. Treat every backing service as a swappable attached resource behind a single URL/DSN env var. Never commit a `.env` (only `.env.example` with empty values), and never write persistent state to the local filesystem.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: config must live in the environment, not in the repo
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
fail=0
for f in $(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM); do
  case "$f" in
    *.env.example|*.env.sample|*.env.template) continue ;;
    .env|*/.env|.env.*|*/.env.*) echo "12factor III: $f is committed config; move it to the environment" >&2; fail=1; continue ;;
  esac
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  if grep -nEi '(postgres|mysql|mongodb|redis|amqp)(\+srv)?://[^[:space:]\"'\'']*:[^[:space:]@\"'\'']+@' "$f"; then
    echo "12factor III: hardcoded credentialed DSN in $f" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
exit $fail

pool.name: CUPID — for joyful coding
pool.origin: Daniel Terhorst-North (Dan North), 10 Feb 2022; follow-up to his talk "Why Every Element of SOLID is Wrong"
pool.whatItIs: North's replacement for SOLID: five *properties* rather than principles — Composable, Unix philosophy, Predictable, Idiomatic, Domain-based. The core argument is that principles are binary compliance checks, whereas properties define a centre to move toward, so code can be closer to or further from joyful without ever being "non-compliant".
pool.concreteDirective: Structure and name code after the problem domain rather than after framework layers: the top level of a codebase should read like its use cases (e.g. `patient_history`, `appointments`, `staffing`, `compliance`), not like a generated skeleton of `models/`, `views/`, `controllers/`, `helpers/`. Prefer domain types over primitives and computer-science containers (`Surname`, `Money{Currency, Amount}` over `string[30]` / raw floats). Keep each module doing one thing well with a small, intention-revealing surface and minimal dependencies (Composable + Unix philosophy). Make behaviour predictable: code should do what its structure and naming say it does, deterministically and observably. Follow the idioms of the language, its ecosystem and the local codebase (documented in ADRs, enforced by shared formatting and linting) over personal preference. Note: the specific banned-name list (`utils`, `helpers`, `common`, `misc`, `shared`, `*Manager`, `*Processor`, `*Service`) and the "no I/O in a function whose name promises a pure computation" rule are house extrapolations — North argues against layer/framework-shaped structure, and does not enumerate forbidden identifiers.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: block new grab-bag modules (applies to ADDED files only)
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
new=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=A || true)
[ -z "$new" ] && exit 0
fail=0
for f in $new; do
  case "$f" in
    */utils/*|*/util/*|*/helpers/*|*/misc/*|*/common/*) echo "cupid: new grab-bag directory in $f; name it for the domain" >&2; fail=1 ;;
  esac
  b=$(basename "$f")
  case "$b" in
    utils.*|util.*|helpers.*|helper.*|misc.*|common.*|*Manager.*|*manager.*) echo "cupid: new grab-bag module $f; name it for the domain" >&2; fail=1 ;;
  esac
done
exit $fail

pool.name: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (catalog)
pool.origin: Martin Fowler, PoEAA (Addison-Wesley, 2002); free online pattern catalog on martinfowler.com
pool.whatItIs: The naming authority backend engineers actually cite: Domain Model ("an object model of the domain that incorporates both behavior and data") vs Transaction Script, Service Layer, Data Mapper vs Active Record, Repository ("mediates between the domain and data mapping layers using a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects"), Unit of Work ("maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates the writing out of changes"), Identity Map, Lazy Load, Optimistic/Pessimistic Offline Lock.
pool.concreteDirective: Use these pattern names only when the thing matches the catalog definition. A `Repository` "mediates between the domain and data mapping layers using a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects" — so it MUST NOT expose SQL strings, query builders, ORM entities, or `Session`/`EntityManager` types in its signatures; if it does, it is a Table Data Gateway, Row Data Gateway, or Data Mapper, and should be named accordingly. Unit of Work "maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates the writing out of changes AND the resolution of concurrency problems" — quote the full definition, since the concurrency half is what distinguishes it from a plain change buffer. Own the transaction boundary in one Unit of Work at the use-case / Service Layer level, never inside a repository method; a use case that opens two transactions is a bug unless an ADR says otherwise. Choose Transaction Script ("organizes business logic by procedures where each procedure handles a single request from the presentation") for genuinely procedural CRUD and say so — do not build an AnemicDomainModel and call it DDD.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: repositories must not leak persistence types
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -iE '(repository|repositories)' | grep -viE '(adapters?|infrastructure|infra)/' || true)
[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0
fail=0
for f in $files; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  if grep -nEi '(SELECT[[:space:]]+.*[[:space:]]FROM[[:space:]]|EntityManager|QueryBuilder|Session\(|createQuery|knex\.)' "$f"; then
    echo "poeaa: $f is named a Repository but exposes persistence machinery" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
exit $fail

pool.name: Strangler Fig Application
pool.whatItIs: The canonical alternative to the big-bang rewrite: put an interception layer in front of the legacy system, grow the new system around it by taking over one capability at a time, run both in parallel, and remove the old path only once nothing routes to it. Fowler's framing is that rewrites are high-risk and that gradual replacement keeps the system releasable at every step.
pool.concreteDirective: Prefer gradual replacement over a cut-over rewrite of a running system; Fowler's position is that big-bang replacements are "overflowing with risk" and "go down in flames most of the time", and that gradual displacement is "one of those things that isn't tried enough" — treat a full rewrite as requiring an explicit ADR that argues against the strangler fig, not as a default option. The named mechanism is Event Interception: put a façade/router at the boundary first, migrate exactly one capability behind it per change, keep the legacy path live and reachable until traffic for that capability is 100% on the new path, and only then delete the old code in a separate commit. Accept transitional architecture that lets the new and legacy systems coexist; Fowler argues the reduced risk and earlier value outweigh building code that will later be thrown away. Every strangling step must be independently releasable and revertible by flipping routing — if a step cannot be rolled back by routing alone, it is too big.

pool.name: CQRS (with the Event Sourcing caveats)
pool.origin: Martin Fowler, bliki (CQRS coined by Greg Young from Bertrand Meyer's CQS); companion entry Event Sourcing at https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/EventSourcing.html
pool.whatItIs: Fowler's write-up of separating the read model from the write model, notable mainly for how hard he argues against reaching for it: "you should be very cautious about using CQRS"; "for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity"; "the majority of cases I've run into have not been so good, with CQRS seen as a significant force for getting a software system into serious difficulties". He scopes it to a single bounded context with a demonstrated read/write asymmetry, and notes CQRS does not require Event Sourcing.
pool.concreteDirective: Default to a single model for reads and writes. Introduce CQRS only inside one bounded context, only with a measured read/write asymmetry (differing load, differing shape, or differing consistency requirement) recorded in an ADR, and never as a system-wide style. Do not couple CQRS to Event Sourcing: adopt event sourcing only when the audit log or temporal query is itself a product requirement, and when you have written down the schema-evolution and replay strategy for old events. If asked for "CQRS" without that justification, propose the single-model design and say why.

pool.name: Release It! stability patterns (Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Timeouts, Fail Fast)
pool.origin: Michael T. Nygard, Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, Pragmatic Bookshelf (1st ed. 2007, 2nd ed. 2018)
pool.whatItIs: The catalog of stability antipatterns (Integration Points, Cascading Failures, Chain Reactions, Blocked Threads, Slow Responses, Unbounded Result Sets) and the patterns that stop them: Timeouts on every remote call, Circuit Breaker to fail fast when a dependency is sick, Bulkheads to partition resources so one failure cannot drain the whole process, Fail Fast, Handshaking, Steady State, and Back Pressure. Circuit Breaker entered mainstream practice from this book via Netflix's Hystrix.
pool.concreteDirective: Every outbound network call must set an explicit finite connect timeout AND read/total timeout — never rely on the library default, which is usually infinite. Wrap each remote dependency in a circuit breaker and a bounded connection pool sized per dependency (bulkhead), so a slow dependency cannot exhaust the shared request threads. Retries must be bounded, jittered, and applied only to idempotent operations. Bound every query result set with an explicit LIMIT/pagination — an unbounded `SELECT *` over a user-growable table is a production incident waiting for its data volume.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: remote calls without an explicit timeout
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
fail=0
for f in $(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '\.(py|js|ts|tsx|go|rb)$' || true); do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  if grep -nE 'requests\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)\(' "$f" | grep -qv 'timeout='; then
    echo "release-it: $f has a requests call without timeout=" >&2; fail=1
  fi
  if grep -nE '(^|[^.\w])fetch\(' "$f" | grep -qvE 'signal|AbortSignal\.timeout'; then
    echo "release-it: $f has a fetch() without an AbortSignal timeout" >&2; fail=1
  fi
done
exit $fail

pool.name: Evolutionary Database Design & Parallel Change (expand / migrate / contract)
pool.origin: Martin Fowler & Pramod Sadalage (2003, updated 2016); Parallel Change written by Danilo Sato on martinfowler.com, 13 May 2014 — https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ParallelChange.html; book: Refactoring Databases (Ambler & Sadalage)
pool.whatItIs: The practice of treating the schema as versioned, continuously-integrated code: every change is a small, named, forward-only database refactoring checked into the repo and applied automatically. Parallel Change is the safety mechanism for backward-incompatible changes — "breaking the change into three distinct phases: expand, migrate, and contract" — so incompatible schema or interface changes ship with zero downtime.
pool.concreteDirective: Every schema change is a new, immutable, forward-only migration file — never edit a migration that has been applied anywhere, and never write a manual `ALTER` outside the migration directory. Split any backward-incompatible change into three separately deployed steps: EXPAND (add the new column/table/field, nullable, dual-write), MIGRATE (backfill and move all readers over), CONTRACT (drop the old). A `DROP COLUMN`, `DROP TABLE`, `RENAME`, or `SET NOT NULL` may never ship in the same release as the code change that stopped using it.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: destructive DDL must be an explicitly labelled contract-phase migration
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
migs=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '(migrations?|db/migrate)/' || true)
[ -z "$migs" ] && exit 0
fail=0
for f in $migs; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  if grep -qiE 'drop[[:space:]]+(column|table)|rename[[:space:]]+(column|table|to)|set[[:space:]]+not[[:space:]]+null' "$f"; then
    grep -qiE 'phase:[[:space:]]*contract|expand-contract|parallel[- ]change' "$f" || {
      echo "parallel-change: $f contains destructive DDL; ship it as a separate contract-phase migration and mark it 'phase: contract'" >&2
      fail=1
    }
  fi
done
exit $fail

pool.name: RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (with the Idempotency-Key header)
pool.origin: IETF, RFC 9457 (July 2023, Standards Track, obsoletes RFC 7807); companion IETF HTTPAPI WG draft "The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field" at https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/
pool.whatItIs: RFC 9457 standardises machine-readable API errors as `application/problem+json` with the members `type` (a URI identifying the problem type), `title`, `status`, `detail`, and `instance`, plus extension members and an IANA registry — so APIs stop inventing a new error envelope per endpoint. The Idempotency-Key draft standardises the client-generated key ("a UUID or a similar random identifier") that makes POST/PATCH retries fault-tolerant.
pool.concreteDirective: Return every 4xx/5xx as `Content-Type: application/problem+json` (RFC 9457; `application/problem+xml` is the XML equivalent) with a stable `type` URI (defaulting to `about:blank`), a `title` that per RFC 9457 SHOULD NOT change from occurrence to occurrence except for localization, the numeric `status`, and a human-readable `detail` — never a bespoke `{error: "..."}` shape, and never a stack trace or SQL fragment in `detail` (RFC 9457 Security Considerations warn against leaking implementation internals). Register project-specific problem types rather than inventing ad-hoc `type` URIs; IANA maintains an "HTTP Problem Types" registry (Specification Required). Persist key → (request fingerprint, response) and replay the stored response verbatim on retry; the draft only says fingerprints MAY be used and the resource SHOULD reply with the result of the previously completed operation, so treating both as MUST is a project hardening, not a spec quote. Follow the draft's status codes: 400 when a required `Idempotency-Key` is missing, 409 when the original request is still in flight, and 422 (not a generic 4xx) when the same key is reused with a different request payload — each rendered as a problem detail. Document the key expiration policy (the draft says the resource SHOULD define one). pool.origin: Kent C. Dodds, quoting Sandi Metz's 'The Wrong Abstraction'
pool.whatItIs: The counterweight to dogmatic DRY: duplicate code until the shape of the abstraction is proven by real, differing use cases, then extract. Sandi Metz's line is the load-bearing quote: 'prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction'.

pool.name: Colocation
pool.whatItIs: 'Place code as close to where it's relevant as possible.' Tests, styles, types, sub-components, state, and fixtures live next to the module they serve, not in parallel global `__tests__/`, `styles/`, `types/` trees. Do not create a top-level `__tests__/`, `styles/`, `types/`, or `interfaces/` tree mirroring `src/`. Promote a module to a shared folder only when a second feature actually imports it — never in anticipation. Lift state to the lowest common ancestor of its consumers and no higher; if only one subtree reads it, it does not belong in a global store or a root provider.

pool.name: WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024)
pool.whatItIs: The normative accessibility standard. Nine new success criteria over WCAG 2.1. Legally referenced by EN 301 549 (EU), Section 508 (US), and the European Accessibility Act. Verified normative text: 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large-scale text (>=18pt, or >=14pt bold); 1.4.11 requires 3:1 for UI component boundaries and graphical objects against adjacent colors; 2.4.7 requires a visible keyboard focus indicator; 2.5.8 requires targets to fit a 24x24 CSS px square with five exceptions (Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, Essential); 1.4.10 requires no loss of content or function at 320 CSS px width (vertical scroll) or 256 CSS px height (horizontal scroll), i.e. 400% zoom on a 1280px viewport.
pool.concreteDirective: Treat these five AA criteria as ship blockers on every screen you emit: body text >=4.5:1 and large-scale text (>=18pt or >=14pt bold) >=3:1 against its actual background; every control border, icon, focus ring and chart mark >=3:1 against adjacent color; every focusable element has a visible focus indicator; every pointer target fits an axis-aligned 24x24 CSS px square or clears 24 CSS px center-to-center from adjacent targets (Spacing exception); the page reflows at 320 CSS px wide with zero horizontal scrolling. Never emit a viewport meta tag containing user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1 — suppressing pinch zoom removes the resize mechanism 1.4.4 depends on and is a documented WCAG failure pattern (it does not by itself decide 1.4.10, which is judged by reflow at 320 CSS px).
pool.famousBecause: The single standard that every accessibility law, procurement contract, and audit in the world points at. WCAG 2.2 reached W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023 and was re-published 12 December 2024.

files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -Ei '\.(html|jsx|tsx|vue|svelte|astro)$')
[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0
if echo "$files" | tr '\n' '\0' | xargs -0 grep -nEi 'user-scalable[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*(no|0)|maximum-scale[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*1([^0-9.]|$)' 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "BLOCKED: viewport disables zoom (WCAG 1.4.4 / 1.4.10)"; exit 1
fi
exit 0

pool.name: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible + 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured + 2.4.13 Focus Appearance

pool.concreteDirective: Never write `outline: none` or `outline: 0` without a `:focus-visible` rule in the same stylesheet that restores an indicator of at least 2px thickness at >=3:1 contrast against both the component and its background. Use `:focus-visible`, not `:focus`, so pointer users do not see rings. When you add a sticky header, sticky footer, or fixed overlay, add `scroll-margin-top`/`scroll-margin-bottom` equal to that element's height on focusable content so a focused control is never entirely hidden behind it (2.4.11). Never use `outline: none` on `<body>` or `*`.
pool.famousBecause: WCAG 2.2's headline additions; 2.4.11 is the criterion most often failed by the sticky-header pattern that nearly every modern site ships.

fail=0

  echo "$f: outline removed with no :focus-visible replacement (WCAG 2.4.7)"
  fail=1
done
exit $fail

pool.whatItIs: Level AA, new in WCAG 2.2. pool.name: Lighthouse CI
pool.whatItIs: Runs Lighthouse on every commit and asserts against thresholds. Configured via `.lighthouserc.json` with `ci.collect` (staticDistDir or startServerCommand, numberOfRuns) and `ci.assert` (a `preset` plus an `assertions` map). Verified: the `lighthouse:recommended` preset asserts a perfect score on every non-performance audit and warns when metric scores drop below 90; assertions take the shape `"categories:accessibility": ["error", { "minScore": 0.9 }]` where the first array member is "error" or "warn". `lhci autorun` chains collect + assert + upload and exits nonzero on any error-level failure. Lighthouse's accessibility category is itself axe-core, so this is axe with a score attached.
pool.concreteDirective: Commit a `.lighthouserc.json` with `"assert": { "preset": "lighthouse:recommended", "assertions": { "categories:accessibility": ["error", {"minScore": 1}], "categories:performance": ["error", {"minScore": 0.9}], "cumulative-layout-shift": ["error", {"maxNumericValue": 0.1}], "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", {"maxNumericValue": 2500}] } }` and run `lhci autorun` as a required CI check. Set `numberOfRuns: 3` — a single run's performance numbers are too noisy to gate on. Do not treat a 100 accessibility score as compliance: it is an axe subset and still misses roughly half of WCAG. CI only; never a pre-commit hook.
pool.famousBecause: Google's own quality gate; the Lighthouse score is the number every stakeholder already recognizes, which makes it the easiest budget to get organizational buy-in for.

pool.name: pa11y-ci
pool.origin: Pa11y team (Nature Publishing Group origins), LGPL-3.0
pool.whatItIs: A URL-list accessibility runner built for CI. Config lives in `.pa11yci` (JSON, or a CommonJS .js module) with a `urls` array plus per-URL `actions`. Verified: `--threshold <number>` permits N errors before failing with exit code 2 (default 0). Underlying pa11y defaults to the HTML_CodeSniffer runner with WCAG2AA as the default standard (WCAG2A / WCAG2AA / WCAG2AAA are the valid values), and also supports axe via the `runners` array — so you can run both engines in one pass and get union coverage that neither gives alone. Per-URL entries in `urls` may be objects that override any pa11y option, so use `actions` there (`click element #x`, `wait for element #y to be visible`) to reach states behind interaction. CI only — it launches one headless Chrome via Puppeteer and opens an isolated incognito browser context per URL (`useIncognitoBrowserContext` defaults to true, `concurrency` defaults to 1).

pool.name: Stylelint
pool.whatItIs: The CSS linter. Verified rules that directly catch design-system drift: `declaration-property-value-allowed-list` (allowed property/value pairs), `declaration-property-unit-allowed-list` (allowed property/unit pairs — e.g. font-size may only use rem), `unit-allowed-list`, `function-disallowed-list`, `property-disallowed-list`, `color-no-hex`, `color-named`, `declaration-no-important`, `custom-property-pattern`, `selector-max-specificity`, `max-nesting-depth`. pool.name: stylelint-declaration-strict-value
pool.whatItIs: A stylelint plugin that forces named properties to be expressed as variables, functions, or an explicit allowlist rather than literal values — the single most direct mechanical defense against design-token drift. Verified options: primary option is a property list (strings or regex), secondary options include `ignoreVariables`, `ignoreFunctions`, `ignoreValues`, `ignoreAtRules`, `expandShorthand`, `recurseLonghand`, `autoFixFunc`. Recognizes CSS custom properties `var(--x)`, SCSS `$x`, Less `@x`, and css-loader `@value`.
pool.concreteDirective: Enable `scale-unlimited/declaration-strict-value` on `["/color$/", "/^background/", "font-size", "font-family", "z-index", "border-radius", "box-shadow", "/^margin/", "/^padding/"]` with `{ ignoreValues: ["transparent","inherit","currentColor","none","0"], expandShorthand: true }`. This makes a raw `#3b82f6` or a magic `z-index: 9999` a build failure rather than a review comment. Exempt exactly one file — the token definition layer (`tokens.css`, `theme.css`) — and nothing else.
pool.famousBecause: The plugin most design-system teams reach for once 'please use the tokens' stops working as a social convention.

# pre-commit: no raw hex colors outside the token layer. Zero deps.
css=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -Ei '\.(css|scss|sass|less)$' | grep -Ev '(tokens|theme|variables|palette)')
[ -z "$css" ] && exit 0
hits=$(echo "$css" | tr '\n' '\0' | xargs -0 grep -nEi '#[0-9a-f]{3}([0-9a-f]{3}([0-9a-f]{2})?)?\\b' 2>/dev/null)
if [ -n "$hits" ]; then
  echo "$hits"
  echo "BLOCKED: raw hex color outside the token layer. Use var(--color-*)."; exit 1
fi

pool.name: Playwright visual comparisons (toHaveScreenshot)
pool.whatItIs: Built-in, zero-cloud visual regression: `await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` writes a baseline PNG on first run and pixel-diffs against it thereafter using pixelmatch. Verified options: `maxDiffPixels`, `maxDiffPixelRatio`, `threshold`, `stylePath` (inject CSS to mask volatile content), and the `--update-snapshots` flag to re-baseline. Verified caveat, quoted from the docs: 'Browser rendering can vary based on the host OS, version, settings, hardware, power source (battery vs. power adapter), headless mode, and other factors' — so baselines must be generated in the same container CI uses, or every run is a false positive.
pool.concreteDirective: Generate and store all screenshot baselines inside the official Playwright Docker image (`mcr.microsoft.com/playwright`), never on a developer laptop, and commit them. Set `expect: { toHaveScreenshot: { maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01 } }` globally, use `stylePath` to disable animations and hide timestamps/avatars, and capture each component in light and dark by driving `page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' })` and `{ reducedMotion: 'reduce' }`. CI only — screenshot baselines must never gate a commit. Delete flaky snapshots rather than raising the threshold until it hides real regressions.
pool.famousBecause: The first credible visual-regression system that needs no SaaS account, no token, and no vendor — it ships in the box with Playwright.

pool.name: Chromatic
pool.origin: Chromatic (built by the Storybook core team)
pool.whatItIs: Cloud visual-review service that turns every Storybook story into a visual test, renders it across Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge in its own infrastructure, and blocks the PR on unreviewed visual diffs. Runs on every push in CI, requires a project token, and offers TurboSnap to only re-snapshot components affected by a diff. Percy (github.com/percy/cli, now part of BrowserStack; `percy exec -- <test command>`) is the equivalent framework-agnostic alternative, and BackstopJS is the self-hosted one. All three are cloud-or-CI, none are commit-time.
pool.concreteDirective: If the project already has Storybook, wire Chromatic as a required CI check and treat every accepted visual diff as a deliberate design decision recorded in the PR — that is the actual value, not the pixel diffing. Never put a Chromatic or Percy token in a hook, a client bundle, or a committed file; it lives only in CI secrets. If the project has no Storybook and no budget for a SaaS tier, use Playwright toHaveScreenshot or BackstopJS instead rather than adding a component-explorer dependency purely to get visual testing.
pool.famousBecause: Built by the Storybook maintainers, so it is the default visual-review answer for the ~most-adopted component workshop in frontend.

pool.name: BackstopJS
pool.whatItIs: Self-hosted visual regression testing driven by a single `backstop.json` config listing scenarios (url, selectors, viewports, interaction scripts). Renders with headless Chrome and also supports Playwright and Puppeteer engines. Ships an in-browser diff report UI, CLI and JUnit reporters, and integrated Docker rendering specifically to make screenshots reproducible across machines. Zero cloud dependency and no token — the right choice for a harness that prefers not to depend on a vendor.
pool.concreteDirective: Define scenarios per component state, not per page, and always set `viewports` to at least 320px (to prove WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow) plus your standard breakpoints. Run `backstop test` through the Docker rendering option in CI so baselines are byte-stable; `backstop approve` is the only way a baseline changes, and that command must never run in CI. Add `misMatchThreshold: 0.1` rather than 0 to absorb subpixel antialiasing noise.
pool.famousBecause: The original open-source visual regression runner, predating the SaaS generation, and still the reference implementation for doing it entirely inside your own CI.

pool.name: prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-color-scheme and the color-scheme property
pool.origin: CSS Working Group / W3C, documented by MDN
pool.whatItIs: Two user-preference media features plus the CSS property that makes dark mode actually work. `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` signals a user who has enabled OS-level motion reduction (macOS Accessibility > Motion, Windows Ease of Access, iOS, Android, GNOME); ignoring it is a vestibular-disorder hazard and maps to WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions. `prefers-color-scheme: dark|light` reports the OS theme. Separately, the `color-scheme` CSS property (Baseline widely available since Jan 2022) tells the UA which schemes an element supports and is what restyles scrollbars, form controls, and the canvas surface — a dark theme built only from `prefers-color-scheme` media queries still renders white scrollbars and light native inputs. The `light-dark()` function collapses paired values into one declaration.
pool.concreteDirective: Ship a global reduced-motion escape hatch in every stylesheet — `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; animation-iteration-count: 1 !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; scroll-behavior: auto !important; } }` — and never gate essential information or state changes on an animation. For theming, always set `:root { color-scheme: light dark; }` and add `<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">` in the head so native controls and scrollbars follow the theme and there is no white flash on load. Define the full light palette on bare `:root` and override only the tokens inside the dark block — a color whose only definition lives inside a media query breaks in the other theme. Re-verify 1.4.3 and 1.4.11 contrast separately in dark mode; a palette that passes in light routinely fails inverted.
pool.famousBecause: prefers-reduced-motion is the rare accessibility feature with a hard clinical justification (vestibular disorders) and universal browser support since January 2020; the missing `color-scheme: light dark` is the single most common defect in hand-built dark modes.
pool.shellGate:
# pre-commit: motion added with no prefers-reduced-motion escape hatch anywhere in the repo.
css=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -Ei '\.(css|scss|sass|less)$')
[ -z "$css" ] && exit 0
added=$(git diff --cached -U0 -- $css | grep -E '^\+' | grep -Ei '(animation|transition)[a-z-]*[[:space:]]*:')
[ -z "$added" ] && exit 0
if grep -rql 'prefers-reduced-motion' --include='*.css' --include='*.scss' --include='*.less' . 2>/dev/null; then
  exit 0
fi
echo "BLOCKED: motion declared but the repo has no prefers-reduced-motion block (WCAG 2.3.3)"
exit 1

unverified.name: Derek Yu — PIXEL ART TUTORIAL: BASICS
unverified.origin: Derek Yu (creator of Spelunky, co-founder of TIGSource)
unverified.whatItIs: The classic end-to-end walkthrough of building a single sprite: line art, jaggies, selective outlining, anti-aliasing, light source, palette size, dithering. It is the tutorial that popularised the term 'selout' outside the Pixelation forum.
unverified.famousBecause: The most-linked pixel art tutorial on the English-speaking internet for roughly two decades, written by the author of Spelunky.
unverified.concreteDirective: Apply these five rules verbatim while placing pixels: (1) jaggies are line segments whose lengths do not grow or shrink consistently — fix by making run-lengths monotonic, and accept that minimisation not elimination is the goal; (2) anti-alias with in-between colours only at corners where segments meet, and scale the AA run to the segment run — 'the longer the line segment, the longer the segment of AA'; (3) never anti-alias the outer silhouette when the background colour is unknown, because the halo will show against a different background; (4) selout means replacing pure black outline with lighter shades where light hits, dropping the outline entirely where the sprite meets negative space, and using a darker shade for internal segmentation; (5) fix one light source above and slightly forward, so tops and fronts are bright and bottoms and backs are dark.

unverified.name: Derek Yu — PIXEL ART: COMMON MISTAKES
unverified.whatItIs: The companion piece naming the four failure modes that kill small sprites: too many similar colours, naive colouring, pillow shading, and cardboard (grid-locked, flat) designs. It states the 'Chunky Pixels Rule' explicitly.
unverified.famousBecause: The standard reference for critique vocabulary in pixel art communities — 'pillow shading' and 'banding' as review terms come largely from here and from Pixelation.
unverified.concreteDirective: Before committing a sprite, verify all four: (1) every colour has its own identity — if two swatches blend at 1x, delete one; (2) no naive colour — do not use pure #00FF00 for a leaf or pure grey for stone, vary saturation and brightness from observation; (3) no pillow shading — shading must never run from the outline inward with light in the centre and dark on every edge; (4) obey the Chunky Pixels Rule: avoid rendering any feature with only a single pixel of thickness, and think in forms with volume rather than lines. Banding is when thick uniform bands of colour make the eye focus on the boundary lines rather than the colours — break it by interlocking the ramp steps or by a 2-colour dither, not by adding a third band.

unverified.name: Les Forges Pixel Art Course (Ch. 2 Lines and Curves)
unverified.origin: Fil Razorback, LesForges.org; English translation archived on OpenGameArt
unverified.whatItIs: The chapter that defines 'perfect lines' by their coefficients and gives the exact run-length discipline for smooth diagonals and curves. This is the source of the '1-2-3' / '2-2-2' pixel-run guidance in concrete form.
unverified.famousBecause: The Les Forges course is the most complete free structured pixel-art curriculum in English (8 chapters, archived on OpenGameArt); Chapter 2 is the canonical reference for lineart accuracy.
unverified.concreteDirective: Draw every straight edge as a perfect line using one of the coefficients 0:1, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, 1:0 — that is, every step in the staircase has identical length (2-2-2-2 or 3-3-3-3, never 2-3-2). Draw every curve with progressive run-lengths that only ever grow or only ever shrink along the arc (e.g. 5 4 3 2 2 1 1 1, longest runs at the cardinal points, shortest at the 45-degree diagonal) and never place a right angle inside a curve. Treat lineart accuracy as load-bearing: at 32x32 a single stray pixel is ~0.1% of the image but a visible defect at 1x.

unverified.name: Les Forges Pixel Art Course (Ch. 4 Shadow & Light, Ch. 5 Colour Palettes, Ch. 6 Anti-aliasing)
unverified.origin: Fil Razorback, LesForges.org; archived on OpenGameArt
unverified.whatItIs: Chapter 4 fixes the light-source convention and names pillow shading; Chapter 5 states the hue-shift law and the 'Xenodrogen method' for monotonic ramps; Chapter 6 gives the segment-length rule for hand anti-aliasing and the ban on full-contour AA.
unverified.famousBecause: The eight-chapter Les Forges course is one of the few free tutorials that states hue shifting as an explicit directional rule rather than a vibe.
unverified.concreteDirective: Light: place the single light source at top-left or top-right (sun convention) and keep it consistent across every sprite in the set; a secondary ambient light may lift only the *edges* of shadows, never their interiors. Hue shift, stated as a law: as a ramp gets darker, increase saturation and rotate the hue toward blue; as it gets lighter, decrease saturation and rotate the hue toward yellow. Xenodrogen method: hue, saturation and brightness must each change in one direction only across a ramp, with no yo-yo in the rate of change; a 3-colour ramp needs 15-20 units of variation per step, a 5-colour ramp less. Avoid pure black and pure white except for metal, gems, and outlines. AA: add buffer pixels only where two colours meet, one line or column at a time; a 1px segment takes at most two AA pixels, a 2px segment more; never let buffer shades spill past a segment's endpoints (that is what causes banding); never build a contour of AA around the whole shape; do not AA a lone 1px 45-degree step.

unverified.name: SLYNYRD Pixelblog 1 — Color Palettes
unverified.whatItIs: The most numerically specific published treatment of hue shifting: exact degrees of hue rotation per swatch, ramp length, ramp spacing around the wheel, and the saturation/brightness curve shape.
unverified.famousBecause: The Pixelblog series is a long-running, widely cited beginner-to-intermediate pixel art curriculum; entry 1 is the reference people quote for '20 degrees of hue shift per step'.
unverified.concreteDirective: Build every ramp with positive hue shift of roughly 20 degrees per swatch from dark to light (dark end rotated toward blue/violet, light end toward yellow/orange). Space separate ramps ~45 degrees apart around the wheel so eight ramps close the circle and the whole palette stays harmonious. Shape the curve: brightness increases monotonically left to right and never starts at 0; saturation peaks near the middle of the ramp and never reaches 0 or 100; take larger saturation steps at the ends and smaller ones in the middle; take smaller brightness steps as brightness approaches 100. Never combine maximum saturation with maximum brightness. For a 32x32 sprite use 3-4 swatches per ramp, not the full 9.

# pre-commit: 32x32 grid integrity + colour budget + no orphan glyphs

for f in $(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '\.sprite$'); do

  grid=$(grep -vE '^#' "$f")
  rows=$(printf '%s\n' "$grid" | grep -c .)

  grep -Ev '^([^ ]) #[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$' "$p" | grep -q . && { echo "$p: bad palette line (want '<glyph> #rrggbb')"; fail=1; }
  n=$(awk '{print $2}' "$p" | sort -u | grep -c .)
  [ "$n" -le 16 ] || { echo "$p: $n colours exceeds the 16-colour budget"; fail=1; }

  echo "BLOCK[conventional-commits]: '$MSG'" >&2
  echo "  want: <type>[(scope)][!]: <description>  types: ${TYPES}" >&2
  exit 1

unverified.concreteDirective: Write the OpenAPI document and get it reviewed before writing the handler (API-first, [100]). Never break backward compatibility on a published API [106]. Always return a JSON object as the top-level structure, never a bare array [110]. Property names MUST match `^[a-z_][a-z_0-9]*$` — snake_case, never camelCase [118]. Every error response MUST be problem JSON [176]. Every collection MUST be paginated, and cursor-based paging is preferred over offset [159][160]. Use only official IANA status codes [243] and stick to the common subset [150]. Dates and times MUST use RFC 3339 `date-time`/`date`/`time` [169]. unverified.name: Microsoft / Azure REST API Guidelines
unverified.origin: Microsoft (Azure SDK API Stewardship Board; Microsoft Graph guidelines live at vNext/graph/GuidelinesGraph.md)
unverified.whatItIs: Microsoft's prescriptive REST guidance. Note that the historical top-level `Guidelines.md` is now a deprecation notice: the live documents are the Azure REST API Guidelines and the Microsoft Graph REST API Guidelines under `vNext/`.
unverified.famousBecause: Governs the entire Azure and Microsoft Graph surface; the origin of the widely imitated `{"error":{"code","message","target","details","innererror"}}` envelope and of `api-version` date-stamped versioning.
unverified.concreteDirective: Require an `api-version` query parameter on every operation in `YYYY-MM-DD` form (`-preview` suffix for previews) and return 400 when it is missing or unrecognised. Shape every list response as an object `{ "value": [...], "nextLink": "<absolute URL>" }` with `nextLink` omitted on the final page — never a bare array, and never require the client to construct the next-page URL itself. Errors return `{"error": {"code", "message", "target", "details", "innererror"}}` with the top-level `code` mirrored in an `x-ms-error-code` response header. JSON field names are camelCase and case-sensitive; omit null-valued fields entirely rather than emitting `null`. Use RFC 3339 in bodies and query strings, IMF-fixdate in headers. Async work returns 202 with an `Operation-Location` header pointing at a status monitor that is polled by GET. Honour `If-Match`/`If-None-Match`/`If-Modified-Since` and return 304 or 412 as appropriate. Support `Repeatability-Request-ID` plus `Repeatability-First-Sent` on POST. Return 414 when a URL exceeds 2083 characters. NEVER change the meaning of an existing api-version — cut a new date instead.

unverified.name: RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs
unverified.origin: IETF Standards Track (M. Nottingham, E. Wilde, S. Dalal), July 2023 — obsoletes RFC 7807
unverified.whatItIs: The IETF standard media type `application/problem+json` (and `+xml`) for carrying machine-readable error detail in HTTP responses, plus an IANA registry of common problem type URIs.
unverified.famousBecause: The only vendor-neutral standard for HTTP error bodies; mandated by Zalando, adopted by Spring Boot, ASP.NET Core, Redocly and most modern API style guides.
unverified.concreteDirective: Return `Content-Type: application/problem+json` for every 4xx and 5xx response, with members `type` (a stable URI that is the primary machine-readable identifier), `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`. The `status` member MUST equal the actual HTTP response status code. Put every machine-consumable value in a named extension member (e.g. `balance`, `invalid_fields`) — clients MUST NOT parse `detail`, so never encode data only in that prose. Keep `title` constant per problem type across occurrences; only `detail` and `instance` vary. Clients MUST ignore unknown extension members and MUST ignore members whose value type does not match. Use `about:blank` as `type` when the status code alone carries the whole meaning; NEVER invent a `type` URI that does not resolve to documentation you actually publish, and never auto-dereference `type` at runtime. NEVER put a stack trace, SQL fragment, exception class name, internal hostname or credential into `detail`. NEVER ship a second bespoke error envelope (`{"error":"..."}`, `{"success":false}`) alongside problem+json, and never return 200 with an error body. Migrate any RFC 7807 citation in docs or code comments to RFC 9457.
unverified.shellGate: f=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -Ei '(openapi|swagger).*\.ya?ml$'); [ -z "$f" ] && exit 0; for s in $f; do grep -qE "^ *['\"]?[45][0-9X][0-9X]['\"]?:" "$s" || continue; grep -q 'application/problem+json' "$s" || { echo "$s declares 4xx/5xx responses without application/problem+json (RFC 9457)"; exit 1; }; done; exit 0

unverified.name: RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics
unverified.origin: IETF HTTP Working Group (R. Fielding, M. Nottingham, J. Reschke), June 2022
unverified.whatItIs: The current normative definition of HTTP methods, status codes, conditional requests, representation metadata, safety and idempotency. Supersedes RFC 7230-7235.
unverified.famousBecause: It is HTTP. Every argument about 401-vs-403, 400-vs-422, or whether PUT is idempotent is settled by this document.
unverified.concreteDirective: Choose status codes only from the IANA registry — never invent one, and never overload a code to mean something the spec does not say. Use 400 for malformed syntax and 422 for well-formed but semantically invalid content; 401 strictly for unauthenticated and it MUST carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header, 403 for authenticated-but-forbidden; 404 for absent, 410 for deliberately gone; 409 for a state conflict, 412 when an `If-Match`/`If-None-Match` precondition fails, 428 to demand a precondition; 429 with `Retry-After`. Creation returns 201 with a `Location` header; accepted-async returns 202; empty success returns 204 with no body. GET and HEAD are safe and MUST NOT mutate state — never implement a mutation behind GET, not even for a webhook or a convenience link. GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE MUST be idempotent: a client retry MUST NOT double-apply. NEVER return 200 with an error payload, and never return 500 for a client input mistake. PATCH is defined by RFC 5789, not by RFC 9110 — cite it correctly.
unverified.shellGate: if git diff --cached -U0 | grep -nE '^\+.*(status\(200\)|statusCode *[:=] *200|HttpStatus\.OK).*([Ee]rror|[Ff]ail)'; then echo 'returning 200 with an error payload violates RFC 9110 status semantics'; exit 1; fi; exit 0

unverified.name: Idempotency-Key (IETF HTTPAPI draft + the Stripe model)
unverified.origin: IETF HTTPAPI Working Group draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header (Standards Track, latest -07, Oct 2025); prior art documented by Stripe at docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests and stripe.com/blog/idempotency
unverified.whatItIs: A request header field carrying a client-generated opaque key so that a retried POST or PATCH is executed at most once. The draft defines it as an RFC 8941 structured-header String; Stripe's docs and Brandur Leach's write-up are the reference implementation.
unverified.famousBecause: It is how payment APIs avoid charging a card twice; the Stripe implementation is the pattern the entire fintech industry copied, and it is now on the IETF standards track.
unverified.concreteDirective: Accept `Idempotency-Key` on every non-idempotent mutation that moves money, sends a message, or creates a durable side effect. The key is a client-generated opaque string (a UUID) and the client MUST reuse the identical key across every retry of the same logical operation — never generate a fresh key on retry, and never derive it server-side from a payload hash. Persist the tuple (key, request fingerprint, response status, response body) in the SAME database transaction as the business write; a separate write after commit is a lost-update bug. On a replay with the same key and the same fingerprint, return the stored response byte-for-byte. On the same key with a DIFFERENT payload, return 422 and do not execute. On a concurrent in-flight duplicate, return 409. Scope keys per authenticated principal and per endpoint, never in one global namespace. Expire keys on a documented window (Stripe prunes at 24 hours) and document the post-expiry behaviour. NEVER accept the header on GET or DELETE, where it has no effect. NEVER treat a request as idempotent merely because the handler 'looks safe' — persist the key or drop the claim from your docs.

unverified.name: OpenAPI Specification 3.1 (spec-first workflow)
unverified.whatItIs: The current OpenAPI description format. 3.1 realigned the schema object to be a full JSON Schema 2020-12 dialect, which removes several 3.0-only keywords and changes how nullability and examples are written.
unverified.famousBecause: The de-facto interface description language for HTTP APIs; the input format for Spectral, Redocly, oasdiff, and essentially every client generator and mock server.
unverified.concreteDirective: Edit the OpenAPI document BEFORE the handler, and treat it as the source of truth: generate request/response types and clients from it rather than hand-writing DTOs that drift. In 3.1 use JSON Schema 2020-12 spelling — `type: [string, "null"]`, plural `examples: [...]`, numeric `exclusiveMinimum: 5`. NEVER use the OAS 3.0-only forms `nullable: true`, singular `example` inside a schema, or boolean `exclusiveMinimum: true`; they are silently ignored in 3.1 and produce a spec that lies. Give every operation an explicit `operationId`, every response an explicit schema, and never leave a bare `type: object` with no `properties` as a response body. Never hand-edit generated code. Never merge a change to a route, request shape or response shape without the matching spec change in the same commit — a spec that trails the implementation is worse than no spec, because tooling and clients trust it.
unverified.shellGate: changed=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM); echo "$changed" | grep -qE '(^|/)(routes?|controllers?|handlers?|api)/' || exit 0; echo "$changed" | grep -qEi '(openapi|swagger).*\.(ya?ml|json)$' || { echo 'route/handler changed with no OpenAPI change in the same commit: spec-first violated'; exit 1; }; exit 0

unverified.name: Spectral (with Redocly CLI as the alternative linter)
unverified.whatItIs: A JSON/YAML ruleset linter with first-class OpenAPI 3.1/3.0/2.0 and AsyncAPI support. Rulesets are declarative YAML (JSONPath `given` + `then` functions) and can be extended from `spectral:oas`. Redocly CLI covers the same ground with `recommended`, `recommended-strict`, `minimal` and `spec` rulesets.
unverified.famousBecause: The standard way API governance is mechanised; Adidas, Azure and Zalando all publish their style guides as public Spectral rulesets.
unverified.concreteDirective: Check a `.spectral.yaml` extending `spectral:oas` (or a `redocly.yaml` extending `recommended-strict`) into the repo root and run `spectral lint <spec> --fail-severity=error` in both pre-commit and CI. Encode the house style — required `operationId`, snake_case properties, problem+json on every 4xx/5xx, mandatory `description` on every parameter — as machine rules, never as a review checklist a human is expected to remember. NEVER downgrade a rule from `error` to `warn` or `off` to get a specific PR through: either fix the document or delete the rule permanently with a one-line ADR saying why. unverified.name: oasdiff
unverified.origin: oasdiff maintainers (Reuven Harrison; formerly under the Tufin org)
unverified.whatItIs: A Go CLI that diffs two OpenAPI documents and classifies each change. `oasdiff breaking` reports only consumer-breaking changes with an ERR/WARN severity; `oasdiff changelog` produces human-readable release notes. Ships a GitHub Action that posts a PR review.
unverified.famousBecause: The de-facto breaking-change detector for OpenAPI — the REST equivalent of what `buf breaking` is for protobuf.
unverified.concreteDirective: Run `oasdiff breaking <base-spec> <head-spec> --fail-on ERR` on every pull request that touches the specification, comparing against the spec as it exists on the release branch, and block the merge on ERR. Treat these as breaking and therefore forbidden on an existing version: removing an endpoint or operation, removing a response property, adding a required request property or parameter, narrowing an enum, tightening a type or format, changing a success status code, making an optional response field optional-to-absent. Ship any such change through parallel change (add the new field/endpoint, migrate consumers, then remove) or a new version — never as an in-place edit. NEVER pass `--exclude-elements` or an ignore file to silence a real finding; publish `oasdiff changelog` output into the release notes so consumers see every non-breaking addition too. When the binary is absent the gate exits 0 with a notice instead of failing the push.
unverified.shellGate: command -v oasdiff >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo 'oasdiff unavailable; skipping breaking-change check'; exit 0; }; [ -f openapi.yaml ] || exit 0; base=$(git merge-base HEAD origin/main 2>/dev/null) || exit 0; tmp=$(mktemp) || exit 0; git show "$base:openapi.yaml" > "$tmp" 2>/dev/null || { rm -f "$tmp"; exit 0; }; oasdiff breaking "$tmp" openapi.yaml --fail-on ERR; rc=$?; rm -f "$tmp"; exit $rc

unverified.name: Buf — breaking change detection and the Protobuf style guide
unverified.whatItIs: `buf breaking` compares a Protobuf schema against a past state and reports changes that break clients, servers or generated code, grouped into four escalating categories: FILE, PACKAGE, WIRE_JSON, WIRE. `buf lint` enforces the Buf style guide (STANDARD ruleset).
unverified.famousBecause: Buf replaced protoc as the default protobuf toolchain; its category ladder is the standard vocabulary for arguing about what counts as a breaking proto change.
unverified.concreteDirective: Every proto module gets a checked-in `buf.yaml` with `lint.use: [STANDARD]` and `breaking.use: [FILE]` — drop to WIRE_JSON or WIRE only when you genuinely own every client and every persisted message, and record that choice in an ADR. Run `buf lint` and `buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main'` in pre-commit and CI. Style: files are `lower_snake_case.proto`; the package is `lower_snake_case`, mirrors the directory path, and its last component MUST be a version (`foo.bar.v1`); messages and enums are PascalCase, fields `lower_snake_case`; enum values are `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` prefixed with the enum name and the zero value MUST be `<ENUM_NAME>_UNSPECIFIED = 0`; services are PascalCase suffixed `Service`; every RPC has its own `MethodNameRequest`/`MethodNameResponse` message, never shared with another RPC and never a bare scalar or `google.protobuf.Empty`. NEVER reuse or renumber a field number or field name — mark it `reserved`. NEVER change a field's type, move a field into or out of a `oneof`, move a message between files, or delete a field without reserving it. Breaking changes ship as a new package version directory (`v2`), never as an edit to `v1`.
unverified.shellGate: git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -q '\.proto$' || exit 0; command -v buf >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo 'buf unavailable; skipping proto lint/breaking'; exit 0; }; buf lint || exit 1; buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main' || exit 1; exit 0

unverified.name: Shopify GraphQL Design Tutorial + graphql-inspector
unverified.whatItIs: Shopify's public version of the internal schema-design tutorial distilled from years of running a production GraphQL API, written as a numbered rule list. graphql-inspector diffs two GraphQL schemas and labels every change breaking, dangerous or non-breaking, with a CLI and a GitHub Action that fails the PR check.
unverified.famousBecause: The Shopify tutorial is the single most-cited GraphQL schema design document in existence; graphql-inspector is the standard CI gate for GraphQL schema evolution.
unverified.concreteDirective: Design the schema around the business domain — never mirror your database tables, never mirror the current UI screen, and never transliterate a legacy REST endpoint (Shopify rule 3). Expose a field only when a concrete use case demands it: additions are cheap, removals and retypes are breaking. Use enums instead of free-form strings, custom scalars for money/date/id, and object-wrapped mutation payloads carrying a `userErrors` field rather than throwing for expected business failures. Paginate every list with a Relay-style connection, never a bare list field. Run `graphql-inspector diff <deployed-schema> <new-schema>` in CI and fail on breaking. NEVER remove or retype a field without first marking it `@deprecated(reason: "...")`, giving consumers a stated window, and confirming zero usage from operation logs. NEVER change an output field from non-null to nullable, or an input field from nullable to non-null — both break existing clients. NEVER add a required argument to an existing field.

unverified.name: Parallel Change (expand / migrate / contract)
unverified.whatItIs: The named pattern for making a backward-incompatible interface or schema change safely, by splitting it into three separately deployable phases: expand (add the new form, dual-write, read new-then-old), migrate (move data and consumers), contract (remove the old form).
unverified.famousBecause: The canonical reference for zero-downtime schema and API evolution; every 'expand and contract migration' guide traces back to this page.
unverified.concreteDirective: Split every incompatible change into three separate deploys: expand, migrate, contract. NEVER ship a destructive DDL — `DROP COLUMN`, `DROP TABLE`, `RENAME COLUMN`, `RENAME TO`, `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` — in the same deploy as the code that stops using it: during a rolling deploy the previous application version is still serving traffic against the new schema. NEVER rename a column or table in place; add the new one, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, stop writes, then drop in a later deploy. NEVER backfill inside the same transaction or the same migration file as the DDL — backfill in throttled batches outside a transaction. On PostgreSQL, always `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` / `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, always add constraints as `NOT VALID` then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` in a second statement, and always set `lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout` before DDL so a blocked migration fails fast instead of queuing every writer behind it. On MySQL, run any ALTER against a large table through gh-ost (github.com/github/gh-ost, triggerless, binlog-based) or pt-online-schema-change — never a bare blocking `ALTER TABLE`.
unverified.shellGate: mig=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -Ei '(^|/)(db/)?migrations?/'); [ -z "$mig" ] && exit 0; if git diff --cached -U0 -- $mig | grep -inE '^\+.*(DROP +(COLUMN|TABLE)|RENAME +(COLUMN|TO)|ALTER +COLUMN +[a-z_"]+ +(SET +DATA +)?TYPE)'; then echo 'destructive DDL must ship as its own contract-phase deploy (ParallelChange)'; exit 1; fi; exit 0

unverified.name: Squawk (with ankane/strong_migrations)
unverified.origin: Steve Dignam — github.com/sbdchd/squawk; Andrew Kane — github.com/ankane/strong_migrations
unverified.whatItIs: Squawk is a linter for PostgreSQL migrations and raw SQL with ~40 named rules that catch downtime-causing DDL. strong_migrations is the equivalent for Rails, blocking dangerous ActiveRecord migrations in development and printing the safe rewrite.
unverified.famousBecause: The two tools that turned 'we took the site down with a migration' into a lint error; strong_migrations' README is the most-cited catalogue of unsafe Postgres/MySQL operations.
unverified.concreteDirective: Run `squawk` over every new `.sql` migration in pre-commit and CI. Keep these rules enabled and never blanket-exclude them: `ban-drop-column`, `ban-drop-table`, `ban-drop-not-null`, `ban-drop-database`, `renaming-column`, `renaming-table`, `changing-column-type`, `adding-required-field`, `adding-field-with-default`, `adding-foreign-key-constraint`, `adding-serial-primary-key-field`, `constraint-missing-not-valid`, `disallowed-unique-constraint`, `require-concurrent-index-creation`, `require-concurrent-index-deletion`, `ban-concurrent-index-creation-in-transaction`, `prefer-robust-stmts`, `prefer-text-field`, `prefer-timestamptz`, `prefer-bigint-over-int`, `prefer-identity`, `require-lock-timeout`, `require-statement-timeout`, `transaction-nesting`. In Rails, install strong_migrations and follow its printed safe rewrite: to drop a column, first add it to `ignored_columns` and deploy, then drop in a later migration; to rename, add-new / dual-write / backfill / switch reads / drop. NEVER wrap a migration in `safety_assured` or set `SAFETY_ASSURED=1` without a comment naming the reviewed reason and the lock analysis. NEVER silence a squawk finding with a repo-wide `--exclude`; use a scoped `-- squawk-ignore <rule>` comment with a justification on the single statement.

unverified.name: Transactional Outbox pattern
unverified.origin: Chris Richardson, microservices.io pattern catalogue (Microservices Patterns, Manning)
unverified.whatItIs: The pattern for atomically updating a database and publishing a message: the service inserts the event into an `outbox` table inside the same local transaction as the state change, and a separate message relay (polling publisher, or transaction-log tailing via CDC such as Debezium) publishes it to the broker.
unverified.famousBecause: The standard answer to the dual-write problem; the backbone of event-driven microservices and of every 'we lost events during a deploy' postmortem.
unverified.concreteDirective: NEVER publish to a message broker from inside a request handler, and never inside or immediately after a database transaction — a dual write drops messages whenever the broker call fails after commit or the process dies between the two. Insert the event row into an `outbox` table in the SAME transaction as the business state change, and let a separate relay process publish it (polling publisher, or CDC / transaction-log tailing). Every event carries a stable event id, the aggregate id as the partition key, a type name and a schema version. Delivery is at-least-once, so every consumer MUST be idempotent: dedupe on the event id in an inbox table before applying. NEVER assume ordering across different aggregates — only per partition key. NEVER delete or mark an outbox row as published before the broker has acknowledged it. NEVER expose internal database column names or an ORM entity as the event contract: define the event schema explicitly and version it under the same breaking-change rules as your API.

unverified.name: OpenTelemetry Semantic Conventions (with RED and USE)
unverified.origin: OpenTelemetry / CNCF (semconv); RED — Tom Wilkie at Weaveworks; USE — Brendan Gregg (brendangregg.com/usemethod.html)
unverified.whatItIs: The stable registry of attribute names and span-naming rules for HTTP, database, messaging and RPC telemetry — the first OpenTelemetry conventions declared stable, which renamed roughly 17 HTTP attributes from their pre-1.0 forms. RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) and USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) are the two standard metric checklists layered on top.
unverified.famousBecause: OpenTelemetry is the CNCF-wide instrumentation standard, and semconv is what makes a dashboard portable across vendors; RED and USE are the two most-cited monitoring methodologies in SRE practice.
unverified.concreteDirective: Emit only the stable attribute names: `http.request.method`, `http.response.status_code`, `url.full`, `url.path`, `server.address`, `http.route`, `error.type`. NEVER emit the pre-stable names `http.method`, `http.status_code`, `http.url`, `net.peer.name` — during a migration set `OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=http/dup` and then cut over to `http`. Server span names are `{method} {http.route}` (`GET /orders/{orderId}`) and MUST NOT contain a raw URL, a resource id, an email, or any other high-cardinality value; when no low-cardinality route template is available, use the method alone. NEVER place a user id, access token, password, PII or a full query string into an attribute — scrub `url.path` and `url.query`. NEVER invent a custom attribute where a registry attribute already exists; genuinely new ones get your own namespace prefix. Every service exports RED per route (request rate, error rate, duration histogram — histogram, never an average) and USE per resource (utilization, saturation, errors) for CPU, memory, connection pools and queues.
unverified.shellGate: if git diff --cached -U0 | grep -nE '^\+.*["'\'']((http\.(method|status_code|url))|net\.peer\.(name|port))["'\'']'; then echo 'pre-stable OTel attribute name: use http.request.method / http.response.status_code / url.full / server.address'; exit 1; fi; exit 0

unverified.name: Google SRE Workbook — Implementing SLOs
unverified.origin: Google SRE (The Site Reliability Workbook, O'Reilly); companion chapters: sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/ and sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/
unverified.whatItIs: The chapter that defines SLIs as good-events / valid-events, SLOs as a target over a rolling window, the error budget as 1 minus the SLO, and multiwindow multi-burn-rate alerting. The error-budget-policy chapter supplies the written escalation contract.
unverified.famousBecause: The source of the entire SLO/error-budget vocabulary used across the industry, and of the specific 14.4x/1h, 6x/6h, 1x/3d burn-rate alert ladder.
unverified.concreteDirective: Define every public API operation's SLI as good events divided by valid events, measured as close to the client as possible — never from a server-side average, and never from an internal-only probe. State each SLO as target plus rolling window (`99.9% of GET /orders return < 300ms over 28 days`) and write down the error-budget policy that says exactly what stops when the budget is exhausted (feature freeze, release halt, reliability work prioritised). Alert on multiwindow multi-burn-rate — 14.4x over 1h, 6x over 6h, 1x over 3 days — and NEVER page on a raw resource threshold like `CPU > 80%`, on a single failed synthetic probe, or on any signal a user cannot feel. NEVER set an SLO at 100%: with no error budget there is no room to deploy. NEVER let a new endpoint take production traffic before its SLI is wired and its dashboard exists. Review and re-tune targets on a stated cadence rather than treating the first number as permanent.

unverified.name: Effective React Query Keys (query key factories)
unverified.origin: Dominik Dorfmeister (TkDodo), TanStack Query maintainer — part 8 of the React Query blog series
unverified.whatItIs: The canonical key-design pattern: keys are structured most-generic → most-specific (`['todos'] → ['todos','list'] → ['todos','list',{filters}] → ['todos','detail',id]`), built by a single `as const` factory object per feature, colocated in `features/<X>/queries.ts` alongside the hooks.
unverified.famousBecause: The query key factory is now standard in essentially every serious TanStack Query codebase and is reproduced verbatim in the official docs' community-patterns section.
