Call `get_variable_defs` first to pull the selection's actual variables and styles (colors, spacing, typography), map each one to an existing token in the codebase, and only then call `get_design_context`; any variable with no code counterpart is a decision to surface, not to hardcode. Run `create_design_system_rules` once per repo to write the design-system rules file the agent reads on every subsequent generation. Use `get_code_connect_map` so a Figma component resolves to the real component in the repo rather than a fresh reimplementation. Generate one frame or one component at a time — Card, Header, Sidebar — and if generation feels slow or stuck, reduce the selection size rather than the expectations. The server has no knowledge of your naming conventions or component usage patterns: treat it as a junior engineer who needs context, not as magic.
unverified.famousBecause: The industry-standard design-to-code bridge; `get_variable_defs`-before-codegen is the accepted way to stop agents from hardcoding hex values that a design token already names.

Figma recommends three sections — general coding rules (layout preferences, code organization), design system guidelines (component usage, styling, spacing), and detailed component specs (variants, usage patterns, visual styles) — and supports multiple uploaded .md files or auto-generating guidelines by analysing the project's npm packages and library styles.
unverified.concreteDirective: Keep the always-on guidelines file to the smallest set of rules that actually change output, and audit it for contradictions before adding to it. Figma's own stated limit: 'More context isn't always better. It can confuse the LLM. Try and add the most important rules you need.' Structure it in exactly three tiers — general coding rules, design-system rules, then per-component specs — and push everything below tier one out of the always-on file. Reference real component names and real token names in prompts so the model has something concrete instead of guessing at brand identity, and break a large design goal into several smaller prompts rather than asking for a whole product at once.

unverified.name: AGENTS.md — the open format for agent instructions
unverified.origin: Emerged from OpenAI Codex, Amp, Jules (Google), Cursor and Factory; now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Spec repo: https://github.com/agentsmd/agents.md
unverified.whatItIs: The interoperable, no-required-fields Markdown format that 20+ coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Jules, Aider, Cursor, VS Code, Amp, Factory) read for project context. Over 60,000 open-source projects carry one. Its one real mechanic is scoping: nested AGENTS.md files are supported in monorepos and the closest file to the edited path wins.
unverified.concreteDirective: Scope rules by location rather than piling them into one root file: put a species' rules in the directory that species governs, and rely on nearest-file-wins resolution so a backend commit never pays the token cost of frontend typography rules. Keep the root file to project overview, build/test commands, code style and security considerations, and let each nested file override only what it must. Treat the file as instructions the user's own prompt is allowed to override — never as a policy the agent enforces against the user.

unverified.name: WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation)
unverified.whatItIs: The normative accessibility standard, and the source of the numeric thresholds every design rule in this space quotes. WCAG 2.2 added the criteria that most AI-generated UI fails: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), and 2.4.13 Focus Appearance.
unverified.concreteDirective: Treat these as binary ship gates, not aspirations. Contrast: 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text (≥24px regular / ≥18.66px bold), and 3:1 for UI component boundaries and graphical objects (1.4.3, 1.4.11). Target size: every pointer target at least 24×24 CSS px unless an equivalent alternative or sufficient spacing exists (2.5.8). Focus: never remove an outline without replacing it — a visible `:focus-visible` indicator is mandatory, must not be obscured by sticky headers or bars (2.4.11), and must itself meet 3:1 (2.4.13). Motion: anything that auto-moves, blinks, scrolls or auto-updates for more than five seconds needs pause/stop/hide (2.2.2), and every animation needs a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` path (2.3.3). Text resizes to 200% without loss of content (1.4.4), and reflows at 320px width without two-dimensional scrolling (1.4.10).

unverified.name: APCA — Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm (Myndex)
unverified.origin: Andrew Somers / Myndex Research; the contrast method developed for WCAG 3 (npm: apca-w3, colorparsley)
unverified.whatItIs: The perceptual replacement for the WCAG 2 contrast ratio, reporting a lightness contrast value Lc from roughly -108 to 106 that accounts for polarity (dark-on-light vs light-on-dark), font size and font weight. It is the method the leading anti-slop design skills now specify alongside — or in place of — the 4.5:1 ratio, because WCAG 2's ratio mis-scores dark-mode and mid-tone pairs that look obviously wrong.
unverified.concreteDirective: Score every (color, background-color) pair on the page, not just the ones you remember declaring: body text under 24px regular or 18px bold needs APCA Lc ≥ 60 (or WCAG 4.5:1); large text, icons and focus rings need Lc ≥ 45 (or 3:1). Use OKLCH lightness as a cheap pre-check — if |L_text − L_bg| < 50% the pair probably fails — then confirm with a real calculation via `apca-w3`. Catch the three pairs that ship broken most often: text inside a card that inherits `color` while the card switched to a different surface token; muted text on a raised surface; and a fill that got an accent background without its paired `--color-accent-ink`. Any rule that sets a background at OKLCH lightness < 50% must set its text color in the same rule.

unverified.famousBecause: The contrast method WCAG 3 is being built on, and the one named explicitly by Hallmark's contrast gates and by most published anti-slop rule sets.

unverified.name: Anthropic canvas-design skill
unverified.whatItIs: Anthropic's official skill for producing visual art (posters, covers, .png/.pdf canvases) rather than UI. It ships 25+ OFL-licensed display faces (Boldonse, Bricolage Grotesque, Gloock, Italiana, Young Serif, Big Shoulders, Pixelify Sans, Silkscreen…) and runs in two phases. Its sibling for generative work is https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/algorithmic-art/SKILL.md
unverified.concreteDirective: Split art into two phases and never skip the first. Phase 1: write a design-philosophy .md that names an aesthetic movement and states its principles of form, space, color and composition — specific enough to direct the work, loose enough to leave interpretive room. Phase 2: express that philosophy on the canvas at 90% visual and 10% essential text, with text integrated as a visual element rather than explanatory blocks. Hard constraints: nothing overlaps, every element sits inside the canvas with real margins, limited and cohesive palette, vast negative space, thin typography, sophisticated abstraction over literal cartooning. On refinement, never add graphics — ask 'how can I make what is already here more of a piece of art?' Create original work; never reproduce an existing artist's style as a copy.
unverified.famousBecause: First-party Anthropic, and the clearest published statement of the philosophy-then-execution split that separates a designed artifact from a generated one.

formatLessons: @-IMPORTS ORGANIZE BUT DO NOT SAVE CONTEXT. Anthropic states it plainly: 'Splitting into @path imports helps organization but doesn't reduce context, since imported files load at launch.' obra/superpowers puts it more sharply — '@ syntax force-loads files immediately, consuming 200k+ context before you need them' — and forbids @-links inside skills entirely, requiring '**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** <name>' by name instead. Consequence for Harnemon: the AGENTS.md @-import list IS the always-on budget. Only deletion, path-scoping, or demotion to a skill reduces it.

A RULE IS ADVISORY; ONLY A HOOK IS ENFORCEMENT — AND THE VENDOR SAYS SO. Anthropic: CLAUDE.md and rules are 'context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead'; and 'Settings rules are enforced by the client regardless of what Claude decides to do. CLAUDE.md instructions shape Claude's behavior but are not a hard enforcement layer.' The corollary is a deletion rule: any always-on line containing 'before every commit', 'after each edit' or 'always run X' is proof that the constraint was filed under the wrong pillar.

A SKILL DESCRIPTION MUST DESCRIBE ONLY THE TRIGGER, NEVER THE WORKFLOW. This is the highest-value and least-obvious FORM lesson found, and it is empirically derived. From superpowers/writing-skills: 'NEVER summarize the skill's process or workflow' — testing showed an agent whose skill description said 'code review between tasks' performed ONE review, even though the skill body's flowchart specified TWO; changing the description to pure triggering conditions made the agent read the body and comply. 'Descriptions that summarize workflow create a shortcut agents will take. The skill body becomes documentation agents skip.' Write: 'Use when <symptoms, contexts, error strings>' and stop.

A checked-in harness rots at the URL level, and this research produced two live examples: microsoft/api-guidelines' top-level Guidelines.md is now only a deprecation notice pointing at azure/ and graph/, and RFC 7807 was obsoleted by RFC 9457 in 2023. Every cited URL in a rule needs a verified-on date, and the harness needs a periodic link-check, or the agent will follow a dead standard with full confidence.

A directive is only hook-able if it names a literal string. 'Never inline a queryKey array', 'use client must be line 1', 'no createStore(', 'no XContainer.tsx' all convert to a one-line `git diff --cached | grep '^+.*<literal>'` gate. 'Prefer good abstractions', 'colocate related code', 'set an appropriate staleTime' cannot ever become gates and must stay in rules. When drafting a rule line, write it so the forbidden token is quotable — that single editing habit decides whether the rule gets a hook.

A test-verification harness needs an explicit evidence clause in a rule, because exit code 0 is the single most common false signal an agent acts on. The rule must demand the runner's own summary line (passed/failed/skipped counts) be pasted, and must require zero skipped and non-zero test count — otherwise `.only` and an empty suite both read as success.

AN UNINDEXED SKILL IS A DEAD SKILL — CURATION IS A FORMAT REQUIREMENT. Progressive disclosure means only names and descriptions are resident, so a skill absent from skills/INDEX.md is invisible regardless of how good it is (Nimbleet already calls this a 'dark skill'). The curation lists model the row format: hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code (github.com/hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code) and PatrickJS/awesome-cursorrules (github.com/PatrickJS/awesome-cursorrules) both use one line per entry with a name, a one-line 'what/when', and a link. Make INDEX.md a three-column table — Skill | Trigger / When to use | Location — and gate it in a hook: for every skills/*/SKILL.md, the directory name must appear in INDEX.md or the commit fails.

An always-on art rule should be a short list of invariants an agent must hold while placing every single pixel, not a curriculum. The genuinely always-on set is about eight lines: silhouette first, one light source, hue-shift both directions, 8-16 colours, no pillow shading, consistent run-lengths, no dithering at this size, check on both #ffffff and #000000. Everything else (ramp construction, AA segment maths, palette hexes, eye anatomy) is on-demand and belongs behind a skill trigger.

Anti-pattern rules must name the replacement in the same sentence as the ban, and the hook's failure message must repeat it. 'No arbitrary waits' produces a stuck agent; 'no arbitrary waits — use expect.poll, a web-first assertion, or await findBy*' produces a fix. Every banned API needs a named successor at the point of refusal.

Any skill added here must be registered in skills/INDEX.md in the same commit or it becomes a dark skill that never loads. The INDEX row needs a trigger column written in the same concrete-noun vocabulary as the skill's own frontmatter description, otherwise the router and the skill disagree about when to fire.

Anything whose violation is a single grep on a staged diff belongs in hooks/, not rules/. URL path versioning, pre-stable OTel attribute names, destructive DDL in a migration, a handler changed without its spec - each is a three-line pre-commit that proves itself once, versus a rule line that spends tokens on every single turn restating something no one disputes.

Anything with a template or a worked example goes to `skills/`, and the rule keeps only the trigger sentence plus the path. ADR sections, C4 notation checklists, the aggregate-design walkthrough, and the PoEAA pattern catalog are all lookup material that blows past the 100-line cap the moment you include one example. The rule says WHEN to open the skill; the skill carries the HOW.

Attribution is what makes a grep gate survive contact with a team. A bare 'BLOCK: secret found' sends the developer hunting; `src/bad.py:1:q = "SELECT ..." + user_id` is actionable. The awk helper that tracks `+++ b/<file>` and parses the `@@` hunk header for the starting line number costs four lines and turns a hook from annoying to useful — verified working in my test repo.

Canon that is a caveat needs default-deny phrasing plus a named escape hatch, or the agent reads the pattern name as an endorsement. Fowler's CQRS entry is four paragraphs of warning, yet "CQRS" in a rule file reads as "use CQRS". Write it as "Default to a single model; CQRS only inside one bounded context with the asymmetry recorded in an ADR" — the escape hatch is what keeps the rule from being ignored when the rare legitimate case arrives.

Collapse the four layering canons into ONE always-on rule file. Cockburn (Hexagonal), Martin (Clean), Palermo (Onion) and the DDD layered architecture are the same constraint stated four ways — Uncle Bob's own 2012 post says so explicitly. Shipping four near-identical `rules/*.md` files triples the always-on token cost and adds zero enforceable directives. Write `rules/dependency-direction.md` (~45 lines) stating the direction once, and cite all four URLs inline on the lines they justify.

Compress reference tables to one line per entry and push rationale to the skill. The Radix 12-step mapping is 12 lines when written as 'N — job'; it is 60 lines when each step gets its explanation. The rule owns the mapping, the skill owns the why. Never state the same number in both places or they drift.

Contracts that bind two species - Problem Details, Idempotency-Key, status-code semantics, the pagination envelope - must live in one shared rule file that both Harnemons reference, never copied into each. A duplicated contract drifts, and a drifted contract is more dangerous than no contract because both sides still believe it holds.

Cross-species seams need one definition in a shared rule, not two drifting copies. The FE/BE contract (Pact pact shape, the MSW handler set that mirrors it) is consumed by both the frontend and backend species — duplicating it into each species' rules directory guarantees they disagree within a month.

DESCRIPTIONS MUST BE DELIBERATELY PUSHY, BECAUSE AGENTS UNDER-TRIGGER. Anthropic's own skill-creator says so outright: 'currently Claude has a tendency to "undertrigger" skills — to not use them when they'd be useful. To combat this, please make the skill descriptions a little bit "pushy"', with the worked fix appending '…Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions X, Y, or Z, even if they don't explicitly ask for a "<thing>".' Note the tension with the previous lesson and resolve it correctly: widen the TRIGGER surface aggressively, never leak the STEPS. Every Harnemon skill description should end with an explicit widening clause.

Diff-scanning grep gates have one dominant bug, and I hit it live: `git diff --cached | grep '^+'` leaves the `+` marker on the line, so any pattern containing `+` (string-concat detection, the core SQL-injection signal) self-matches and fires on EVERY added line. My first SQL gate reported 3/3 false positives for exactly this reason. Every generated hook must strip the marker before matching — `awk '/^\+/ { print substr($0,2) }'` or `sed 's/^+//'`. Bake this into a shared `added()` helper in each Harnemon's hooks/ so no individual gate can get it wrong.

Directives are only useful if they are testable at the pixel level. 'Use hue shifting' is unenforceable; 'the shadow swatch must be rotated ~20 degrees toward blue from the base swatch, not merely lower in brightness' can be checked by eye and, for a declared palette, by script. Write every art directive so a reviewer can point at a specific pixel or hex value and say pass or fail.

Do not restate a hook's contents in a rule file. If the pre-commit gate already blocks raw SQL interpolation, the rule should say 'bind parameters; the pre-commit hook enforces this' in one line rather than re-listing the regexes — duplicated content drifts out of sync, and the hook is the authority because it actually executes.

Enforce the 100-line cap by counting directives, not lines. A rule file that has grown past ~15 imperative sentences has stopped being always-on context and become a document; extract the longest three into a skill and leave a one-line router entry. Measure after every edit rather than at audit time, because the growth is always one "just one more clarification" at a time.

Every art hook must degrade gracefully and no-op cleanly. Gate on `git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '\\.sprite$'` so a commit touching no sprites exits 0 immediately, and use only awk/grep/sort/sed so the hook never needs Python, Node, or an image library. A hook that cannot find its palette file should fail loudly with the missing path, not silently pass.

Every gate needs a graceful-degradation guard. Wrap any use of python3/node/jq in `command -v X >/dev/null 2>&1 ||` and pass, not fail, when the tool is absent. A hook that hard-fails on a machine missing a runtime trains people to use --no-verify, which kills every other gate too.

Every hook must open with `command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0`, compute its staged file list first, and `exit 0` immediately when that list is empty. Scope by path prefix (`migrations/`, `doc/adr/`, `domain/`) so the gate is silent on unrelated commits. Prefer plain `for` loops over `xargs -r` and GNU-only flags: `-r` is unavailable on BSD/macOS, and a hook that errors on the maintainer's laptop is a hook that gets deleted.

Every hook must open with a staged-file filter and exit 0 immediately when the filter is empty. `git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '\.(css|tsx)$'` followed by `[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0` is the load-bearing first two lines: a backend-only commit must never pay for a frontend gate. Use `--diff-filter=ACM` specifically so deleted files are not passed to grep as missing paths.

Every hook opens with graceful-degradation lines before it can fail: `command -v npx >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0`, `[ -f package.json ] || exit 0`, and an empty-file-list early exit. A gate that blocks a commit in a repo lacking the toolchain gets deleted by the first frustrated developer, taking the real gates with it.

Every hook that reaches for a tool must degrade to exit 0 when it is absent, and say so. The APCA gate is the model: check `command -v node`, then `node -e "require.resolve('apca-w3')"`, and print 'skipping' rather than failing the commit on a machine that never installed the dev dependency. A gate that fails on a missing tool gets disabled by the first developer it blocks.

Every hook that shells out to a third-party binary must open with `command -v <tool> >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo skipping; exit 0; }`. A pre-commit that hard-fails because squawk, buf or oasdiff is absent blocks contributors who never touched a spec, and the fix people reach for is deleting the hook.

Every mechanical gate needs a documented, greppable escape hatch or developers reach for `--no-verify`, which silently disables the entire hook rather than the one false positive. detect-secrets models this well with inline `pragma: allowlist secret`. Generated hooks should honour a trailing `# harnemon:allow <gate-name>` comment on the offending line and require the gate name, so a blanket suppression is impossible.

Every skill added here (e.g. a hook-authoring playbook, a bundle-budget playbook) must be registered as a row in skills/INDEX.md with an explicit trigger phrase in the same commit that creates SKILL.md. An unregistered skill is a dark skill — present on disk, never routed to, pure dead weight.

Exempt exactly one path per token gate and name it in the script. The raw-hex hook only works because `grep -Ev '(tokens|theme|variables|palette)'` carves out the definition layer; without that the hook fails on the file it is supposed to protect, and the team's fix is to delete the hook. Any design-system gate needs its single legal home for literals written into the gate itself.

Exit-code semantics differ per host and must never be assumed. Git hooks block on any non-zero exit; Claude Code hooks block only on exactly exit 2, and only on the documented blocking events (PreToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop) — PostToolUse cannot block at all because the tool already ran. A hooks/ README in each species should state which host it targets.

Gate placement follows runtime cost, and this should be an explicit three-tier rule in the harness: zero-dependency grep in pre-commit (milliseconds, blocking), Semgrep p/default in pre-push or CI (seconds), CodeQL and full-history TruffleHog in CI only (minutes, never blocking a commit). Putting a minutes-long scanner in pre-commit is the single most reliable way to get the whole harness bypassed.

Gate placement is a latency decision: per-file and fast checks go on pre-commit (lint, format, grep gates); whole-program and slow checks go on pre-push (tsc --noEmit, knip, size-limit, full test suite). A slow pre-commit is bypassed; a slow pre-push is tolerated.

Gate the staged diff, not the working tree. `git diff --cached -U0 | grep -E '^\+'` only judges lines being added, so a repo with pre-existing violations can adopt the hook today. A hook that greps the whole tree is unadoptable in any existing codebase.

Give a skill an explicit safety rail when it edits an existing codebase. Hallmark's is worth copying verbatim in shape: state the exact files you expect to modify/create/delete before editing, require explicit confirmation for any deletion, default to in-place edits or additive components wired through existing routes, and treat READMEs, PDFs and briefs as reference material rather than copy to paste. A design skill that redesigns is one bad inference away from deleting a route tree.

Give escape hatches a literal token instead of writing softer rules. A gate that blocks `getByTestId` or a cross-feature import is only tolerable if there is a documented in-file annotation (`// testid-ok`) that the grep excludes. Binary gates without a named override get disabled wholesale with `--no-verify`, which costs more than the rule was worth.

Grep gates must read the STAGED blob (`git show ":$f"`), never the working tree. Reading the worktree makes partially-staged files pass or fail on content that is not part of the commit — the gate is then simply wrong, in both directions, and wrong silently.

Grep-based gates need a negative-lookahead substitute, because POSIX grep has none. The workable pattern is per-file pairing: find the offending token, then check the same file (or the whole repo, for global resets) for the required counterpart and `continue` if present. The `outline: none` / `:focus-visible` gate and the `animation` / `prefers-reduced-motion` gate are both built this way, and both keep the exemption scope explicit in the script rather than in a config file.

HOOK STDERR IS A MESSAGE TO THE AGENT, NOT A LOG FOR THE HUMAN. disler/claude-code-hooks-mastery documents the contract: exit 0 = success (stdout shown to the user in transcript mode); exit 2 = blocking error where 'stderr is fed back to Claude automatically'; any other code = non-blocking, stderr shown to the user, execution continues. Git hooks are cruder (any non-zero blocks) but the writing lesson transfers exactly: a failing hook should print the file path and the corrective action in imperative voice ('src/Button.tsx: hardcoded #3b82f6 — use var(--color-accent) from tokens/color.css'), because that string is the agent's next instruction.

HOOKS TAKE ONLY BINARY PREDICATES, MUST DEGRADE ON MISSING TOOLS, AND MUST SCOPE TO STAGED FILES. Anthropic separates plain shell hooks from 'prompt-based hooks or agent-based hooks that use a Claude model' precisely because judgment does not belong in a shell script. Zero-dependency POSIX form: open with `set -eu`, then `command -v <tool> >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0` so an absent linter never blocks a commit, then `files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM)` and `[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0` so the hook only ever judges what is actually being committed. One check per hook file. Warnings print and exit 0; only violations exit non-zero.

Hallmark is the proof of the Rule/Skill split at scale: one router SKILL.md over ~150 on-demand reference files (58 gates, 21 macrostructures, 21 themes, ~50 named component archetypes). Nothing enforceable lives in the router. Copy that shape — the always-on file holds posture and the dispatch table; every number lives in a reference the skill loads.

Hook bodies belong in their own executable files under hooks/ or .claude/hooks/, referenced by path — never inlined as shell strings in JSON/YAML config. Inline strings cannot be shellchecked, diffed meaningfully, or unit-tested, and JSON escaping of a regex is where these gates silently break.

Hooks can only gate LEXICAL, binary facts. px-not-a-multiple-of-4, hex-literal-in-token-layer, Tailwind arbitrary-value bracket, box-shadow-without-a-token, generated-file-edited-without-source: all greppable in a pre-commit with zero dependencies. Contrast ratio, optical alignment, hierarchy and 'is this the right elevation' are judgement calls and must NEVER become hooks; a hook that needs a headless browser or a color library will be disabled within a week.

Hooks can only gate machine-checkable binary facts about the sprite files: the grid is exactly 32 rows of 32 characters, the palette file parses as '<glyph> #rrggbb', unique colours are 16 or fewer, every glyph in the grid has a palette entry, an outline strategy is declared, and every hex is inside the declared named palette. Everything the research actually cares about aesthetically (hue shifting, jaggies, pillow shading, banding, silhouette readability) is a judgement call and must not be faked into a hook.

Hooks must be greppable and binary. 'Is this waitFor callback assertion-only?' needs judgement and belongs in a skill; 'does the staged diff add waitForTimeout' is a one-line grep and belongs in a hook. Any gate whose failure message has to say 'consider whether' is misfiled.

Hooks must degrade gracefully, and the degradation must be an explicit early `exit 0`, not an implicit failure. Every hook opens with existence guards: `command -v npx >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0`, `[ -f tsconfig.json ] || exit 0`. A hook that hard-fails because a tool is absent gets disabled with --no-verify within a week, and then enforces nothing at all.

Hooks must exit 0 when their tool is absent, and non-zero only on an actual finding. `command -v gitleaks >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo note >&2` is the whole pattern. A hook that hard-fails because a teammate has not installed a scanner gets removed within a day, taking every other gate with it — the failure mode is total, not partial.

Hooks must read staged content, not the worktree, and must no-op when their tool is absent. Use `git show ":$f"` rather than `cat "$f"` so a partially-staged file is judged by what is actually being committed, and open every hook with `command -v grep >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0`. Avoid `... | while read` loops that set a failure variable — the subshell discards it; write to a temp file or accumulate with a `for` loop over command substitution.

Hooks only get the string-level half. Hallmark's most valuable gates need a rendered page at 320/375/414/768px, an APCA calculation over computed backgrounds, or a judgement about structural fingerprint — none of which a pre-commit hook can do. What survives as a hook is the greppable subset: `transition: all`, `hover:scale-105`, `#000`/`#fff`, `space-x-`, `overflow-x: hidden`, `outline: none` with no `:focus-visible`, banned font families, `background-clip: text` next to a gradient. Put those in the hook and leave the rest as skill checklist items — a hook that cannot decide must exit 0.

Inline the actual numbers into the rule text, never just the URL. An agent editing a stylesheet will not fetch a spec mid-edit, so '24x24 CSS px', '44x44 pt', '4.5:1', 'APCA Lc 60', 'multiples of 8' must appear literally in rules/*.md. A rule that says 'follow WCAG 2.2 target size' is unfollowable; a rule that says '>=24x24 CSS px, or spaced so 24px circles do not intersect' is testable.

Keep the RED-GREEN-REFACTOR loop itself as a three-line rule and put the pressure-resistance material in a skill. The loop is always-on and must cost almost nothing in context; 'what to do when you already wrote the implementation' is long, situational, and only needed when the rule is about to be violated.

Long source documents compress to 4–6 always-on lines, and the rest is a skill. TkDodo's React Query series is 20+ posts; only four directives justify permanent context cost (server state ≠ client state, staleTime is the knob, key factories per feature, never copy data into useState). bulletproof-react's project-structure doc is ~150 lines; the always-on part is the layer order plus the `import/no-restricted-paths` zone config, and the full folder tree belongs in a skill. Budget rules at 30–60 lines and push the tree diagrams, code samples, and rationale down into skills/.

Number your gates and keep the numbers stable. Hallmark cites 'gate 38a', 'gates 40–41', 'gate 8' from inside prose in other files, and its audit verb returns a ranked punch list by gate number. Stable numeric handles make cross-file references cheap and make a hook's failure message point at a specific line of doctrine instead of a vibe.

Numbered-rule corpora compress into an always-on rule file far better than prose does, because the identifier IS the citation. A 40-line Zalando rule can read 'snake_case properties [118]', 'problem JSON on every error [176]', 'no URL path versioning [115]' and stay under the cap; the rationale lives one fetch away. Same trick for AIP numbers and Squawk rule ids. Never paraphrase the rationale into the rule file - cite the number.

One rule file per DECISION MOMENT, not per topic. 'color.md', 'spacing.md', 'type.md' each stay 30-60 lines and load cleanly; a single 'design-system.md' holding Radix's 12 steps plus M3's role table plus the spacing scale blows past 100 lines and gets skimmed. Split by what the agent is about to type, not by what a book chapter is called.

Ordered enumerations belong in rules, unordered judgement belongs in skills. The Testing Library query priority is eight ranked items and fits in a rule as a numbered list an agent can cite by position; the fifteen RTL mistakes need worked before/after code for each and must be a skill. Never compress a ranking into prose — an agent that cannot cite 'rule step 3' will not follow the ordering.

PACKAGE FOR PORTABILITY: AGENTS.md AT THE ROOT, PLUGIN LAYOUT UNDERNEATH. AGENTS.md (agents.md, stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, 60,000+ projects, 20+ tools) is plain markdown with no required fields and is read by Codex, Cursor, Jules, Aider, VS Code and Copilot; Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, so the documented bridge is a CLAUDE.md whose entire content is `@AGENTS.md`. Below that, Claude Code's plugin layout (code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins) puts `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `hooks/`, `agents/` and `commands/` at the PLUGIN ROOT with only `plugin.json` inside `.claude-plugin/` — the documented 'common mistake' is nesting those directories under `.claude-plugin/`. obra/superpowers ships one skills/ tree with per-runtime thin wrappers (.claude-plugin, .codex-plugin, .cursor-plugin, .devin-plugin, .hermes-plugin, .kimi-plugin) — copy that shape rather than forking content per runtime. Validate with `claude plugin validate ./<dir>`.

Pair every prohibition with its sanctioned alternative on the same line. 'Never DROP COLUMN in the deploy that stops reading it - ship expand, migrate, contract as three deploys' is executable. A bare 'never DROP COLUMN' gets creatively routed around, usually via raw SQL that the linter does not parse.

Palette hex tables must live in a skill or a plain data file, never in an always-on rule. AAP-64 alone is 64 hex lines; dropping it into rules/*.md would blow the 100-line cap by itself and burn permanent context on data the agent needs only while drawing. The rule states the constraint ('8-16 colours, hue-shifted, one declared palette'); the skill carries the values.

Phrase always-on rules as import-path and file-location assertions, never as philosophy. An agent can obey "no file under `domain/` may import `prisma`, `express`, or `adapters/`" and can be caught violating it; it cannot obey "depend on abstractions, not concretions". Every line in a rule file should be mechanically falsifiable by reading one file — if you cannot imagine the grep, it belongs in a skill.

Pillar assignment follows enforceability, not topic. A constraint with a binary machine-checkable answer (commit message shape, staged-file grep, bundle byte budget, exit code) belongs in hooks/ — putting it in rules/ spends always-on tokens on something the model can deprioritize. A constraint needing judgment (which type prefix fits this change, whether a dependency is worth its kB) belongs in rules/ or skills/. Never write a rule that merely restates what a hook already enforces.

Pin the edition in every citation. Two of my sources moved under me: OWASP Top 10:2025 superseded 2021 (final Jan 2026, with Injection dropping A03→A05 and Software Supply Chain Failures taking A03), SLSA v1.0 is now formally Retired in favour of v1.2, and gitleaks deprecated `protect`/`detect` in v8.19.0 so any hook copied from an older blog post invokes a hidden alias. Rules should carry the version tag inline (A01:2025, SLSA v1.2, ASVS 5.0.0) so staleness is visible on read rather than discovered on failure.

Prefer 'read the version-matched source' over 'here are the API facts'. Vercel's own managed AGENTS.md block is only ~5 lines and contains almost no Next.js API content — it says 'This is NOT the Next.js you know … Read the relevant guide in node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before writing any code.' Framework facts rot between the rule being written and the agent reading it; a pointer to version-pinned docs does not. Rules that restate a fast-moving framework's API are a liability.

Prefer directives that are binary and numeric over directives that are evaluative. v0's design section is entirely caps and NEVER-clauses (max 5 colors, max 2 families, never purple, never `space-*`, line-height 1.4–1.6) and it is the section that transplants cleanly into both a rule and a hook. Anthropic's 'take one real aesthetic risk you can justify' is equally important but can only ever be a rule. Sort each candidate directive into those two buckets before deciding its pillar.

Prefer write-free CI variants in gates: `biome ci` over `biome check --write`, `--noEmit` over emit. A gate that mutates files can make itself pass by rewriting the thing it was meant to reject, which is indistinguishable from a real pass in the exit code.

Put the canonical URL on the directive line it justifies, not in a bibliography at the bottom. A trailing References section gets skimmed past; an inline `(https://alistair.cockburn.us/hexagonal-architecture/)` next to the one sentence it backs gets followed when the agent or a reviewer disputes the rule. One URL per directive, maximum — a line with three citations is a line that has not decided what it is asking for.

RULE LENGTH IS A MEASURED PARAMETER, NOT TASTE. Two vendors publish hard numbers and they bracket the Harnemon cap: Anthropic says 'target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence' (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory); Cursor says 'Keep rules under 500 lines' and split into composable rules (cursor.com/docs/context/rules). Chroma's Context Rot study across 18 models supplies the mechanism: 'Models do not use their context uniformly; instead, their performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows.' A 100-line hard cap with a 30-60 line target sits safely inside both vendor figures. Enforce the TOTAL always-on budget per species too (~250 lines), not just per-file, because splitting one long file into four short ones saves nothing.

Reserve hooks for binary, path-scoped checks whose false positives are cheap and locally fixable: ADR filename and section headings, a staged `.env`, destructive DDL in `migrations/`, a `requests.get(` without `timeout=`. Rules that need a parser or whole-program analysis (one-aggregate-per-transaction, bounded-context integrity, "is this really a Repository") must stay rules plus a review skill — a hook that guesses gets disabled with `--no-verify` within a week, taking the honest gates with it.

Resist gating what a grep can only approximate. A camelCase-property gate on an OpenAPI file false-positives on OpenAPI's own keywords (operationId, requestBody, securitySchemes). One noisy rule teaches the team --no-verify, which disables every other gate in the same hook file. A gate that is right 90% of the time is worse than no gate.

Rule files should carry an explicit priority tier. The Redux Style Guide is the only major guide that labels every rule Priority A (Essential) / B (Strongly Recommended) / C (Optional), and it is the reason the guide survives contact with real teams: an agent can tell 'reducers must be pure' (never negotiable) from 'use the ducks pattern' (contextual). Copy the tiering, not just the rules — an untiered 60-line rule file reads as 60 equally-weighted absolutes and agents start ignoring all of them.

Rule files should carry thresholds as literal numbers, not as prose. `24x24 CSS px`, `4.5:1`, `3:1`, `320 CSS px`, `2px thick perimeter`, `--max-warnings 0` are directly checkable; 'ensure adequate contrast' is not. The whole reason WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 belongs in an always-on rule rather than a skill is that it compresses to one integer.

Rule length is settled by the field, not by taste: Anthropic's own frontend-design SKILL.md is ~50 lines of pure prose with zero code blocks and zero checklists, and it carries an entire design lane. It gets away with that because it specifies a *process* (plan → critique → build → critique) plus three named negative examples, not an inventory of tokens. A Pixiel rule that tries to enumerate tokens will blow past 100 lines; one that specifies a process will land near 40.

Rule vs skill splits cleanly on whether the content is a fixed enumeration or an unbounded catalogue. OWASP Top 10 is exactly ten named categories and fits a 30-60 line rule as a checklist. ASVS 5.0.0 is hundreds of numbered requirements across three levels and MUST be a skill with the CSV shipped alongside for on-demand grep — pasting it into a rule would blow the 100-line cap by an order of magnitude and burn always-on tokens on requirements irrelevant to 99% of turns.

Rules must state what the tool cannot see, or the agent will treat a green check as compliance. axe-core's own documented figure is ~57% of WCAG issues found automatically, and jsx-a11y's static analysis sees far less than that — it cannot evaluate contrast, focus order, target size, or reading order at all. A one-line 'this gate proves absence of these defects only' clause prevents the failure mode where the agent reports a page as accessible because eslint passed.

SKILL DIRECTORY NAMES ARE PART OF THE SPEC AND PART OF THE TRIGGER. agentskills.io/specification: `name` is 1-64 chars, lowercase alphanumerics and hyphens, no leading/trailing hyphen, no consecutive hyphens, and 'Must match the parent directory name'. superpowers adds the discovery half: name verb-first with gerunds because that is what agents search for — 'creating-skills not skill-creation', 'condition-based-waiting not async-test-helpers', 'root-cause-tracing not debugging-techniques'. So Pixiel gets `designing-tokens`, Reactyl gets `fetching-server-data`, Hexadrake gets `modelling-aggregates` — never `token-system`, `data-layer`, `ddd`.

SKILLS SHOULD BE A/B TESTED AGAINST NO SKILL, AND THE BAR FOR ADMISSION IS A BEHAVIOR CHANGE. Both major sources converge independently. superpowers/writing-skills: 'Writing skills IS Test-Driven Development applied to process documentation… If you didn't watch an agent fail without the skill, you don't know if the skill teaches the right thing' — run the baseline first, record the exact rationalizations the agent produces, then write the skill to close those specific loopholes. Anthropic's skill-creator: spawn with-skill and baseline runs in the SAME turn, save to evals/evals.json, and iterate. DietrichGebert/ponytail (github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail, 115k+ stars) shows the honest version — a headless agent editing a real FastAPI + React repo across 12 tasks, n=4, reporting -54% LOC / -22% tokens, and publicly retracting an earlier inflated single-shot figure. Also borrow ponytail's never-cut list verbatim: trust-boundary validation, data-loss prevention, security and accessibility are exempt from every reduction — which is precisely how Pixiel keeps a11y and Hexadrake keeps validation out of the minimalism blast radius.

Scope every hook by changed path and exit 0 immediately when nothing relevant is staged (`git diff --cached --name-only | grep -q '\.proto$' || exit 0`). Running `buf breaking` on a CSS-only commit is a latency tax, and latency taxes get uninstalled.

Scope every hook grep to the staged diff (`git diff --cached -U0`) and to test-file globs. Scanning whole files makes pre-existing violations block unrelated commits; scanning added lines only means the gate ratchets forward and can be adopted on a legacy repo the day it is written.

Scope rules by path, because the ecosystem already does. AGENTS.md resolves nearest-file-wins across a monorepo (Linux Foundation stewardship, 60k+ repos), and Cursor migrated from a single root `.cursorrules` to `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` files carrying `description` / `globs` / `alwaysApply` frontmatter precisely so a rule loads only for the files it governs (see https://github.com/PatrickJS/awesome-cursorrules and https://cursor.directory). Three species in one repo means three glob-scoped rule sets, not one merged file that every commit pays for.

Scope rules with globs, not with prose conditions. The modern `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` convention that replaced the monolithic `.cursorrules` file exists because one file of rules applied to every path forces the agent to decide relevance on every turn. Split by concern and attach path globs so a backend edit never loads the frontend design rules — the same reason Harnemon rules should stay one-topic-per-file.

Ship skill helper scripts as black boxes and say so in the skill. Anthropic's webapp-testing SKILL.md instructs: 'Always run scripts with --help first… DO NOT read the source until you try running the script first and find that a customized solution is absolutely necessary. These scripts can be very large and thus pollute your context window.' Any Harnemon skill that ships a script needs that same sentence, or the agent will read it into context every run.

Skill `description` frontmatter should trigger on literal artifacts the agent can see, not on abstract security concepts. 'Use when writing SQL, a migration file, a .sql file, an ORM query, or a route handler that reads request.body' fires reliably; 'use when security is a concern' never fires, because the agent does not classify its own turn as security-relevant until after it has written the vulnerable line.

Skill trigger wording must name the ARTIFACT NOUNS an agent will actually see: '.tokens.json', '@theme', 'style-dictionary', 'clamp()', 'oklch(', 'box-shadow', 'design token', 'color scale'. Routing on intentions ('when designing') misses; routing on the strings that appear in the file being opened hits.

Skill trigger wording must name the artifacts and file extensions, not the discipline. A description that says 'pixel art' will not fire when the actual prompt is 'redraw Hexadrake's sprite' or 'the palette looks muddy'. Trigger on the concrete nouns: sprite, 32x32, mascot, palette, hex grid, hue shift, outline, .sprite, .palette, plus the three species names.

Skills registered nowhere are dark skills. Each SKILL.md must land in skills/INDEX.md with its literal trigger strings in the trigger column on the same commit, and that pairing is itself a candidate hook: a staged `skills/*/SKILL.md` with no matching row added to INDEX.md fails pre-commit.

Split 'how to design it' from 'what you may never do', and let that split decide the pillar. The never-list is short, binary and context-free - AIP-180's removal/retype/required-field list, the destructive-DDL list, the pre-stable OTel names - so it goes in rules/. The design walkthrough - modelling a long-running operation, choosing an outbox relay, Shopify's schema tutorial - is long and situational, so it goes in skills/ behind a trigger.

Split the toolchain-dependent gate from the pure-shell gate. `grep` for waitForTimeout runs everywhere with zero dependencies and belongs in pre-commit; `npx eslint` and `vitest run` are slow and environment-dependent and belong in pre-push behind a `command -v` check.

Steal Hallmark's stamp trick: the agent writes its own verification evidence into the artifact as a machine-readable comment — `/* Hallmark · macrostructure: <name> · pre-emit critique: P5 H4 E5 S4 R5 V5 · contrast: pass (40–41) · nav: N# · footer: Ft# */`. A later hook, audit, or the *next* run can grep that stamp to detect a repeated structural fingerprint. Self-verifying output beats a checklist the agent claims to have run.

Strip persona preambles. The dominant form across the 40.7k-star awesome-cursorrules corpus is 'You are an expert in TypeScript, React, and Next.js…' followed by an unranked bullet list. The persona line changes nothing an agent does and the unranked list is unenforceable; the same file's value is entirely in its handful of concrete imperatives ('use nuqs for URL search param state', 'use client only for Web API access in small components'). Keep those, drop the framing.

Structure-enforcing rules need a machine backstop or they decay silently. bulletproof-react does not merely document 'shared → features → app' — it ships the ESLint `import/no-restricted-paths` zones. Encode the rule three ways: the sentence in rules/*.md, the linter config the rule tells the agent to install, and the pre-commit grep. Documentation-only architecture rules are violated within a week and nobody notices.

THE ALWAYS-ON ROUTER RULE IS ITS OWN GENRE, AND IT NEEDS A RATIONALIZATION TABLE. superpowers/using-superpowers is ~60 lines and does exactly four things: sets an invocation threshold ('If you think there is even a 1% chance a skill might apply… you ABSOLUTELY MUST invoke the skill'), orders process skills before implementation skills with two worked examples, requires the agent to announce 'Using [skill] to [purpose]' before acting, and closes with a 12-row Red Flags table mapping each rationalizing thought to the reality that kills it ('This is just a simple question' → 'Questions are tasks. Check for skills.'). The Red Flags table is what makes the rule survive contact with time pressure. Every species needs a domain-specific one.

THE PILLAR TRIAGE HAS PEER-REVIEWABLE EVIDENCE BEHIND IT. arXiv:2606.15828 analysed 100 popular repos and found the three most common configuration smells are exactly the three misroutings the Rule/Skill/Hook matrix prevents: Lint Leakage 62% (mechanically-checkable rules written as prose — belongs in a hook), Context Bloat 42% (always-on content that earns nothing — delete), Skill Leakage 35% (multi-step procedures in the always-on file — belongs in a skill). They cluster together. Run the triage as three questions in this order: Can a regex decide it? → hook. Is it a procedure or scoped to one area? → skill. Would it change nothing in a session where its skill never fires? → delete.

THE THREE-TIER BUDGET IS THE WHOLE ARCHITECTURE, WITH PUBLISHED NUMBERS. Anthropic's engineering post frames it as 'a well-organized manual that starts with a table of contents, then specific chapters, and finally a detailed appendix'. The spec attaches figures: metadata ~100 tokens per skill loaded at startup for ALL skills; SKILL.md body under 500 lines and recommended under 5000 tokens, loaded on activation; references/, scripts/ and assets/ loaded only when required, with 'file references one level deep from SKILL.md' and no deep chains. superpowers tightens tier 1 further with `wc -w` targets: <150 words for getting-started workflows, <200 for frequently-loaded skills, <500 for the rest. Split anything over 300 lines and give it a table of contents.

TRIGGERS BELONG IN THREE PLACES AND EACH HAS A DIFFERENT MECHANISM. (1) Frontmatter `description` — semantic trigger, always resident, ~100 tokens, this is what actually fires the skill. (2) Path globs — Claude Code `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths:` frontmatter and Cursor `.mdc` with `globs:` both load a rule only when a matching file enters context. (3) An always-on router rule listing '<user phrase> → <skill>' mappings, the Nimbleet/superpowers pattern. Use all three: frontmatter for discovery, globs so Reactyl's `app/**/*.tsx` rules never load in a Hexadrake session, and the router for phrases no glob can catch.

The 100-line cap has a citable external justification. Figma's own Make docs state it plainly: 'More context isn't always better. It can confuse the LLM. Try and add the most important rules you need,' plus an instruction to audit guideline files for conflicting information. Prune contradictions before adding lines.

The pre-commit / CI split is the single most important structural fact for these species and must be stated in the rule itself, not buried in a skill. Only three of these tools can ever run at commit time: eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, stylelint, and pure grep. Everything that needs a rendered DOM — axe-core's color-contrast and target-size rules, Lighthouse CI, pa11y-ci, every screenshot tool — needs a browser binary, a build, and a running server, and putting any of them in a pre-commit hook produces a hook developers disable within a week. Write each hook's header comment with the reason it is cheap enough to be a hook.

This body of knowledge is cross-species: the same 32x32 sprite discipline serves Pixiel, Reactyl and Hexadrake. Author it once as a single shared skill plus one shared rule rather than triplicating it into three species directories, where the three copies will drift. Species-specific content is only the design brief (Fairy wings / Sky tail / Dragon horns) and the chosen palette, which are a few lines each.

This research batch feeds Pixiel and Reactyl almost entirely and Hexadrake essentially not at all. Do not manufacture backend relevance to balance the roster — mark axe-core and pa11y-ci as shared because they genuinely gate any server-rendered HTML, and let Hexadrake draw its gates from the architecture, contract, and migration research instead.

Threshold flags are the difference between a gate and a report. `--max-warnings=0`, knip's default exit 1 (not `--no-exit-code`), size-limit's `limit`, `check-added-large-files --maxkb` — the concrete directive in a rule must name the flag and its value, because the tool's default is almost always non-blocking.

Tool-invoking hooks need a two-step absence check, not one. `command -v npx` succeeding does not mean the linter is installed, and `npx --no-install eslint` exits nonzero when the package is missing — which reads as a lint failure and blocks a legitimate commit. Probe with `npx --no-install <tool> --version >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0` first. Graceful degradation means exit 0 with a one-line note, never a false block.

Trigger wording belongs in YAML `description`, never in the body. Superdesign's description is one long sentence packed with the user's own vocabulary and ends '…even if they never say the word design tool'; Hallmark's names its four verbs and the phrases that route to them. The body should be written as if the trigger already fired — restating triggers inside the body wastes tokens and does nothing for routing.

Trigger wording for the a11y skills should name the artifact, not the virtue. 'Writing a tabs / combobox / dialog / menu / tree widget' routes to the APG skill reliably; 'when accessibility matters' never fires, because the agent never believes it does not matter. Same for visual regression: trigger on 'changing a shared component, token, or global stylesheet', not on 'when visual quality is a concern'.

Trigger wording should name the artifact, not the intent. 'When writing a Server Function' misses; 'When a file contains \'use server\'' hits. The most reliable skill triggers observed in the official sources are filename- and token-shaped: `page.tsx`/`route.ts`, `'use client'`, `queryKey:`, `docs/decisions/NNN-*.md`. Intent-shaped triggers ('when architecting') fire inconsistently.

Vercel's stated benchmark finding is the cleanest rule-vs-skill test available: 'always-available context outperforms on-demand retrieval' for framework knowledge, and 'Skills cover the tasks that are workflows rather than lookups.' So: facts and invariants an agent must never violate → rules/*.md; multi-step procedures with checkpoints (adopt a pattern across an app, wire up a form stack, write an ADR) → skills/<name>/SKILL.md.

Verified portability trap worth encoding in a hook-authoring skill: `git grep -E` does not support `\b` word boundaries and matches nothing rather than erroring. A gate built on `\b` reports clean forever. Prefer character-class anchors, `[[:space:]]`, or `git show | grep`.

WRITE INSTRUCTIONS IMPERATIVELY, WITH ONE CLAUSE OF REASONING — NOT STACKED MUSTS. Anthropic's skill-creator: 'Prefer using the imperative form in instructions' and 'Try to explain to the model why things are important in lieu of heavy-handed musty MUSTs.' Anthropic's memory docs give the concreteness test — every rule must be verifiable: 'Use 2-space indentation' over 'Format code properly', 'Run `npm test` before committing' over 'Test your changes', 'API handlers live in `src/api/handlers/`' over 'Keep files organized'. And check for contradictions on every harness edit, because 'if two rules contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily' and arXiv:2606.15828 found Conflicting Instructions clusters with Context Bloat. The one place ALL-CAPS absolutism IS correct is the single fenced Iron Law line per mandatory skill — its scarcity is what gives it force.

Where a rule and a hook cover the same ground, the rule must state the fix, not just the prohibition. 'off-grid px' as a hook message plus a rule that says 'pick a spacing token' resolves in one step; a hook message alone makes the agent round the number blindly and commit a different wrong value.

Write skill `description:` triggers around the artifact and the verb, not the theory. "Use when adding or editing a file under `migrations/`" fires reliably; "use when doing evolutionary database design" never fires, because the agent does not know that is what it is doing. Name the file extension, the directory, or the user's likely words — the theory name goes in the body, not the frontmatter.

Write skill `description` frontmatter out of the literal strings an agent will see in its terminal, not out of topic names. 'Testing' never matches; 'flaky test, waitForTimeout, act() warning, not wrapped in act(...), Unable to find an element with the role, test passes locally fails in CI' matches. Trigger wording is a keyword index, not a summary.

Write skill triggers against artifacts, not intentions. 'When editing a file matching openapi*.yaml, anything under migrations/, or a .proto' fires reliably. 'When designing an API' does not, because the agent does not classify itself as designing an API until the handler is already written and the moment to load the skill has passed.
